speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Pursuant to Standing Order 68(2), the motion is deemed adopted.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to introduce this bill regarding breach of parole.
This bill would amend the Criminal Code to make breach of either parole or statutory release conditions a criminal offence. I believe this amendment could have prevented the murders of Kittye Schmidt and Ezio Faraone.
Schmidt and Faraone were both murdered by parolees who had breached parole conditions. Currently parole officers can issue a warrant for the arrest of parolees who breach conditions.
However as parole officers have limited contact with parolees police officers who patrol the streets are more likely to witness a breach of parole conditions. Currently police officers are unable to arrest a parolee who is breaching non-criminal parole conditions.
This change would go a long way to help protect Canadian people. There is a loophole in the law and this would plug it.

Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition on behalf of several hundred people all over Labrador, where the first Inuk in the history of the legislature of Newfoundland was elected in the person of William Andersen III. I want to offer him my congratulations, and those of the House.
This petition calls upon the government to reverse its decision to cut funding for friendship centres. These have been very important to aboriginal people in Labrador. The funds have been cut and this petition calls upon the government to renew that funding.

May 6, 1993
Routine Proceedings

Madam Speaker, in the first petition, the petitioners request Parliament to ensure that the CRTC carefully regulates the use of foul language and violence in radio and television programming.
They point out that violence is not only acts of violence but can also be language. They feel that neither is necessary to inform or to entertain. They also believe that there is too much violence in society today.
This violence undermines their efforts to bring up their children.

Madam Speaker, in the second petition these petitioners call upon the Government of Canada to remove the hated goods and services tax on books and other reading materials. They point out that it has adversely affected the publishing industry and the creators of these works, such as artists, writers, publishers and what have you.
They also indicate that it runs contrary to government goals of increased productivity and more effectiveness. They point out that reading is essential. It is a cornerstone of a democratic country such as Canada.

Madam Speaker, I rise to present petitions signed by several hundred people from British Columbia asking the federal government to do everything in its power to stop the drift-net fishing in the north Pacific Ocean. They say that we are courting an ecological disaster by allowing drift-net fishing fleets in the north Pacific Ocean and that sea birds and marine mammals are being slaughtered by this practice.
Since the west coast salmon fishery is being damaged and there is a massive impact on our global ecosystem they ask that this Parliament use every means possible to stop the drift-net fishing in the north Pacific, including
the institution of economic sanctions against the offending countries.

Madam Speaker, my second petition is signed by over 400 people who say that the result of violence in entertainment and desensitization to violence in our society is that we are increasingly becoming a culture of violence and violence has become an ordinary part of our children's lives. They say that part of this culture of violence is exemplified by the serial killer board game which portrays torture, rape and murder as fun.
They call on Parliament to consider amending the Criminal Code of Canada so that violent and degrading materials such as these serial killer board games can be kept out of distribution in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Justice, Attorney General of Canada and Minister of State (Agriculture)) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
that Bill C-126, an act to amend the Criminal Code and the Young Offenders Act, be now read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.
He said: Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to lead off the debate in the House on Bill C-126, an Act to amend the Criminal Code and the Young Offenders Act.
This bill is part of a series of measures introduced by the government to protect all members of our society. Its purpose is to reinforce the provisions of the Criminal Code that deal with family violence, child abuse and violence against women in general. The bill will increase protection for victims in general, and more specifically for victims of family violence and for children who are victims of abuse. It will also facilitate admissibility of testimony from children who were abused or who witnessed violence done to others.
I am sure most members will agree that family violence, child abuse and violence against women are among the most pressing and difficult social problems Canada faces today. No child is safe from sexual abuse. Family violence and sexual abuse of children occur at all levels of our society, irrespective of class or income.
The disturbing fact is that victims of family violence and sexual abuse may never come to terms with what happened to them. The physical effects may disappear but the psychological damage remains. These victims may never again be able to trust others as readily as they did before. They may feel insecure for the rest of their lives. The victim is not the only loser. Society is deprived of what would otherwise have been the promising future of this victim as a productive member of the community.
That is why society must take appropriate steps to provide protection against family violence, child sexual abuse and violence against women in general.
Government Orders
Sexual abuse of children and violence against women occur in a situation where the scales are weighted in favour of the aggressor and against the victim. Children are sexually abused by persons who are older and physically stronger than they are. Women are abused and assaulted by men who are both physically and economically stronger. Such acts constitute criminal abuse against individuals who are particularly vulnerable physically or, depending on the aggressor, economically or emotionally vulnerable. As a society we must condemn this kind of behaviour.
The purpose of Bill C-126 is to add to or amend a number of provisions in the Criminal Code. The Criminal Code alone is not enough to protect all potential victims against these crimes. The bill is not intended as the last word in penal reform in this area. More work must be done on crime prevention. In any case, Bill C-126 is, as I see it, a major step in the right direction.

Bill C-126 will introduce a new criminal harassment section to the Criminal Code. The new section is called criminal harassment because we believe this best describes the nature of the crime although the acts are more commonly known as stalking.
More and more cases are being reported of women being stalked by men they used to be involved with and from whom they may be trying to escape.
There have been several cases in Canada recently in which women have been stalked and seriously injured or killed. These cases made it clear that a new provision in the Criminal Code was urgently needed to explicitly criminalize these types of acts.
A recent public opinion survey shows that more than eight in ten Canadians would support a law that would prohibit the persistent harassment and intimidation of another person.
What is commonly called stalking includes such things as repeatedly following someone; spending extended periods of time watching someone's home or place of work; making repeated telephone calls to someone or her friends; making contact with someone's neighbours or co-workers; and contacting and possibly threatening someone's new companion, spouse or children. Any or all of these actions result in the causing of fear for safety.

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
To a certain extent several sections in the Criminal Code already cover the behaviour involved in these cases. These current provisions have been criticized by victims and various groups for several reasons, such as difficulty of proof and inadequacy of coverage. The offence proposed in the bill addresses these concerns.
The new criminal harassment provision would make it an offence for anyone with intent to harass, repeatedly follow or repetitively communicate with another person or anyone known to them, watch or beset where another person or anyone known to them lives or works, or engage in threatening conduct directed at another person or any members of their family if the behaviour causes the other person to reasonably fear for their safety.
I believe we have created a new offence that will capture the sort of behaviour that we, as a society, want to prevent without interfering unjustifiably with anyone's rights or freedoms as guaranteed under the charter.
Undoubtedly, people have the right to move about freely and to communicate freely. But no one has the right to deliberately harass another person in a way that causes the other person to fear for their safety. The bill makes a clear statement that this is a crime.

Groups and individuals involved in the struggle against family violence have pointed out that after an act of family violence at home, it is usually the victim and her children, not the aggressor, who leave the home. There is absolutely no reason that would justify the victim having to leave her home and definitely upset her life.
It has also been mentioned that after being released, men accused of mistreating their wives often return home and harass their victim or assault her again. Again, there is no reason for this to be so.
Bill C-126 seeks to solve these problems by amending the provisions of the Criminal Code concerning release on bail. The bill seeks to codify present practice by providing that the judge can order the accused, as a condition of his release, to refrain from going near a certain place and by requiring the judge, in cases involving physical violence, to consider the possibility of forbidding the accused to communicate with the witnesses, including the victim, or to go near a particular place, such as the family home, explicitly.
Experts say that there is no way to cure sex offenders who go after children and that the treatment given them is intended only to minimize the risks of relapse or repeat offences. Furthermore, the experts say that people who are sexually interested in children tend to occupy positions or have pastimes that give them access to children. The alarming result of this is that once those found guilty of a sexual offence are released, they take advantage of their freedom to prowl around parks in search of children or even to seek a position where they will enjoy the trust of children.
According to some clinicians, sex offenders should be banned for life from situations where they would be likely to commit a repeat offence. The general public has urged the government many times to forbid sex offenders to hold a position where they might have access to children.
To meet these requests, the bill contains a provision which would allow the court to forbid for the period of time it deems appropriate, including life if the judge thinks it necessary, those found guilty of a sexual offence to frequent parks or public bathing areas if children may be found there, child care centres, school yards, playgrounds, community centres and also to hold a job that would put them in a position of trust or authority over children. In any case, this provision would not be mandatory. It would be up to the court to determine if such a ban should be imposed and if so for how long. The court can also change the terms of the ban as the offender's situation develops, which leaves the court some freedom of action.
The bill also adds to the provision of the Criminal Code concerning the obligation to keep the peace. With this addition, someone could obtain a commitment to keep the peace if he or she feared that another person might commit a sexual offence against a child.
Under the new provision, whoever fears that another person might commit a sexual offence against a child under 14 can file a denunciation with a provincial court judge. If the judge is convinced that the denouncer's fears are founded he can order the person named in the denunciation to comply with conditions set by the judge. These conditions include forbidding, for a period of up to 12 months, the person named in the denunciation to
May 6, 1993

engage in activities involving contacts with children under 14 or to be in public places if children might be there.
In this case, it is a preventive measure that could apply to persons never found guilty of a sexual offence, to persons found guilty of a sexual offence before the coming into force of the ban contained in the bill and to sex offenders who were found guilty but not subject to a ban or for whom the ban has expired in some cases.
As a rule, Canadian criminal law applies to criminal acts committed in Canada. Nevertheless, this respect for the recognized principles of international law must be counterbalanced by the sustained interest in child protection. Therefore Bill C-126 is a response to concerns about cases of children taken outside Canada for the commission of what would be an offence in Canada. The bill creates an offence which will not infringe on the sovereignty of other countries. The proposed clause forbids anyone to act for the purpose of taking abroad a child resident in Canada in order to a commit an act of violence or sexual exploitation on that child.
The abduction of children by the father or mother is another important issue. A recent appeal court decision brought to light a deficiency in the protection provided by the present provisions of the Criminal Code. Children are not protected from abduction in cases where the father or mother committing the abduction believes that the custody order is invalid. The bill is intended to correct this deficiency.
We were also concerned about the present provisions on abduction of children by the father or mother. This concern arises from the fact that a battered woman who decides to flee the violence against her, but not against her children, and who takes her children with her could be accused of child abduction. A battered woman should not have to choose between remaining at home or leaving home without her children, for fear of being accused of abduction. Furthermore, recent studies indicate that it is harmful for a child to witness family violence even if the child is not the victim of physical violence.
Government Orders
The bill deals with this problem by offering a defence in such circumstances. The new defence would apply if the father or mother fled for protection from imminent danger and not only to protect the child.
The bill would provide that husband and wife could be found guilty of conspiring with each other. Thus parents would no longer be safe from a conspiracy charge if, for example, they conspired to harm their child.

The bill also contains provisions that will assist child witnesses in testifying about violence or sexual abuse that they have suffered or witnessed.
In 1962 the Supreme Court of Canada decided that in every case in which a child testifies, the judge must warn the jury about the danger of accepting the uncorroborated evidence of a child even where the child testified under oath. The court said that this rule was necessary because of the mental immaturity of the child.
Since 1962 our knowledge of the capacity of children as witnesses has improved greatly. Research has clearly indicated there is nothing inherently fragile in a child's ability to observe and recollect or nothing inherently defective in a child's ability to testify. There is simply no reason to believe that children are automatically less reliable as witnesses than adults. There is therefore no rational reason to always treat children's evidence differently from that of adults.
In 1988 what was then Bill C-15 abrogated the Criminal Code section that required corroboration generally in sexual abuse cases. Nevertheless, because of the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada judges have continued to give the warning in cases involving children.
To correct this situation Bill C-126 proposes to abrogate this route. This would remove the presumption against the evidence given by children. It is important to stress that this proposal would not create a presumption in favour of children's evidence. The judge or jury would evaluate and determine the weight of a child's evidence on an assessment of the child's evidence in the same way as they would an adult's.

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
It is undoubtedly true that testifying in court is an unpleasant and difficult experience for most adults. For children the experience of being a witness can be many times worse. Cases exist in Canada in which children have been so frightened in the witness box that they have been unable to speak or have been physically sick. This already disturbing situation is compounded for young victims of violence and sexual abuse. Indeed, one of the main fears expressed by child victims of sexual abuse is seeing the accused in the court room.
Parliament has already recognized this fact by enacting a provision which provides for the use of a screen or closed circuit television in the court room so the child can testify without seeing the accused. However a problem remains. A person accused, for example of sexual interference, could decide to exercise his right to represent himself. More specifically the accused could decide to represent himself when he is given the opportunity to cross-examine the child victim.
Child abuse occurs in part because of the inequalities between the child and adult in size, knowledge and power. I believe that cross-examination of a child victim by the accused in the adversarial system of criminal law results in a court-sanctioned continuation of that imbalance and abuse and therefore is wrong.
The bill responds to this problem by proposing to permit a judge to appoint counsel for the accused for the sole purpose of conducting the cross-examination of the victim. The accused would remain free to represent himself during the rest of the trial. The bill would prevent the accused revictimizing the child through a personally conducted cross-examination.
The trauma facing a child victim of violence or sexual abuse when he or she appears as a witness in court about what happened can be reduced in another way. The close presence of a person providing emotional support for the child may be critical in reducing the psychological harm occasioned by testifying in court proceedings and can give a young child the reassurance that is required for evidence to be given clearly and confidentially.
The bill proposes to specifically enable a judge to permit a support person of the child's choice to be present and close to the witness while the witness is testifying, even if the public has been excluded. The
proposed amendment would permit the judge to instruct the witness and the support person not to communicate while the child is testifying. In addition, the bill states clearly that the judge may refuse to permit a witness in the case to be a support person.
The bill also proposes changes that would improve that part of the Criminal Code which allows judges to exclude the public from the courtroom. In the bill, the public's right to be present in the courtroom and the interests of child witnesses are reconciled by adding the provision that proper administration of justice includes ensuring that the interests of witnesses under the age of 14 years are safeguarded in cases of violence or sexual abuse.
I elaborated quite a bit on this bill because I believe it will have a positive effect. As I said earlier, family violence and child abuse are complex social evils. Unfortunately, amendments to the Criminal Code will not eliminate them altogether.
However, I believe this bill demonstrates our commitment to guaranteeing the safety of Canadians and to protecting those who are particularly vulnerable. As a society, we must protect the most vulnerable individuals in that society and put an end to criminal abuse of power. These provisions will provide law enforcement agencies and the courts with more and better ways to protect women and children against violence and abuse.
We cannot allow the status quo to continue, where a woman's life may be destroyed by a stalker or a violent spouse.
We cannot allow the status quo to prevent us from doing everything in our power to protect one more child against the evils of sexual abuse. We know that many cases of family violence and child sexual abuse often occur in the family environment, an environment that is familiar and very close to the children. Given those circumstances, we must be careful how we intervene through the judiciary.
We intend to do more work on crime prevention in the months to come. We will develop a national strategy that, with the help of instruments included in the Criminal Code, should make it possible to provide for
May 6, 1993

immediate intervention in cases of violence and to further refine that strategy in the long term.
I hope that with the generous co-operation of members on both sides of the House we will be able to adopt this bill very quickly. That is why I am pleased to move adoption of Bill C-126 at the second reading stage.

Madam Speaker, I listened with interest to the words of the hon. Minister of Justice. I thank him and his department for bringing this legislation forward. If there were something to do better I would suggest it is a little late; it should have come forward earlier.
I also congratulate the member for Moncton and the member for New Westminster-Burnaby for bringing forward their private members' bills. They were both very good private members' bills and have been on the Order Paper for quite some time.
On behalf of our party, we will certainly co-operate with the government and do everything we can to see that this bill receives swift passage. However we are not going to deny groups who want to comment before a legislative committee the opportunity to do so. We feel it is important that this bill go before a legislative committee so that we have the input. We can have all the discussion possible on a particular subject, but until it is in writing, until it is in a form to provide a common denominator for the people of Canada, these people are not going to be able to comment on the same subject exactly. We want to be talking about the same thing.
Now that we are talking about the same thing, it is vital that we have this legislation before a legislative committee. However on saying that I want to assure the Minister of Justice we are going to try to get this bill through a legislative committee as quickly as possible because we want this legislation. We want it with some amendments, but nevertheless we want it. We think it is basically a good piece of legislation and we want to see it dealt with.
I want to go over this bill because it is significant in that it is not just a stalking law. It is law that deals with many other things of interest. I want to talk about the bill
Government Orders
and make some comments on it. It is vital we fully understand the legislation and what it seeks to achieve.
First, the bill creates a new offence of criminal harassment which would prohibit anyone with the intent to harass from repeatedly communicating with or following another person or anyone known to that person. It would also include watching where a person or anyone known to them lives or works or engaging in threatening conduct directed at that person or any member of that family. It would increase the maximum penalty for this offence to five years in prison.
The fact of the matter is we are talking now about a new charge of criminal harassment which would take the place of the term we use of stalking, the reason being that we want to put it in legal language that can lead to convictions. Currently many of the activities usually associated with stalking are covered by the code. The problem has been that the burden of proof is very high and the victims of stalkers have traditionally had a difficult time convincing police they had reasonable grounds to fear for their safety. That has been a very serious handicap.
Women who have been stalked for years in many incidents have not been able to convince police and the judiciary they have been in fear of their lives. Women who have been stalked will say, and with every justification, that they have been through a tremendously horrendous experience. A woman who is stalked does not know if the stalker is going to appear before her in a supermarket, jump out in front of her from behind a tree, speak to her children on the way home from school, make phone calls at all hours of the day or night, send flowers and do everything that will throw the most absolute fear into the victim.
This is not only for a weekend. This is not only for a month. In many cases this is for years. The absolute terror and anxiety felt by the victim can only be imagined by someone who has undergone the actual stalking experience.
With respect to bail conditions, this legislation provides that as a condition of bail a judge may impose a condition that the accused not go near a particular place, the family home for instance. This improves upon section 515 of the Criminal Code in which the judge can only require the accused to stay in a particular place but not stay away from a place.

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
In situations of family violence where physical violence is involved, the judge must consider imposing the bail conditions that the accused not go near a particular place and that he not communicate with any witnesses, including the victim. Judges and the judiciary in this country have to be more sensitive to victims of stalking, and in this case to the charge of criminal harassment. They have to understand what is involved. In that regard I want the government and the provinces of this country to initiate judicial training on this subject to educate the judges on what is involved and on the mind-set of these stalkers and the thought processes and the thinking of the victims.
Hear, hear.

It has to be done or we are not going to get the full benefit of what the government is putting forward today.
There are other matters before the House today in respect to Bill C-126. I just want to go over them, if I may.
One provision is that the Criminal Code would be amended so that a husband and wife would be found guilty of conspiring with each other. Currently a husband and wife are taken to be one person and therefore not capable of conspiring together. This amendment is designed to offer more protection to children under the criminal law.
Currently children are not protected from abduction where there is a valid custody order that the abducting parent honestly believes to be invalid. It is a question of the reasonable belief of the abducting parent. This bill would change that.
It would also cover women who are being battered and who take their children with them when they flee. If the children are not being battered along with their mother then the mother could be charged with abduction under the present law for taking them with her. This amendment to the Criminal Code would allow for a defence in these circumstances. It is unreasonable, no matter how much a woman fears for her safety, that she would leave without her children. To think that woman was actually
abducting these children is stretching a point quite considerably.
The Criminal Code already states that anyone convicted of a sex offence and who is found loitering in or near a school, park, playground or swimming area, commits a summary conviction offence of vagrancy. Under this proposed legislation this section would be changed. This section under the Criminal Code as it stands now has been found unconstitutional by the B.C. Court of Appeal. Change is actually thrust upon us.
This unconstitutional finding by the B.C. Court of Appeal was on the grounds that a lifetime ban without recourse is unfair. This decision, I might add, is under appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. There are many who, in addition to the finding of the B.C. Court of Appeal, also feel that the charge of loitering as it stands at the present time is really too vague.
Bill C-126 would allow for up to a lifetime ban on convicted sex offenders from frequenting day care centres, school grounds, playgrounds or community centres, public parks or bathing areas where children are likely to be found and from seeking or obtaining employment that involves a position of trust or authority over children. The court would have the discretion to tailor the prohibition to each individual, or in some cases where the court felt this was unwarranted to not impose the prohibition at all.
This legislation, as the Minister of Justice has also stated, deals with child witnesses, which is very important.
If we are talking about child abuse, we are talking about litigation and we are talking about parents before the courts. Therefore it is natural that these children be expected to testify.
It is a frightening experience for many adults to go to court. One can just imagine the trauma that children go through, particularly if these court appearances are delayed. Sometimes there is a long period of time between the time of the actual act of child abuse or whatever takes place and the time that the matter comes to court. Sometimes it can be a year and sometimes more.
May 6, 1993

The child is rethinking this horrible experience. This thought of the horrible experience which the child has endured is compounded by the fact that the child has to go before the court, face the person who did this in many cases and testify before a large number of people.
In many cases the child actually believes that he or she is going to be the one put in jail. They feel that they have committed a crime by allowing some adult or some young offender to sexually assault them. This is a tragic situation. Those young people, those young minds are hurt by this thinking of an abuse that was upon them but for which they take full blame. We have to deal with this. We have to set these children's minds at ease. We must have a good body of law and a good procedure before our courts. We have to do it with the interest of the child in mind. We have to. A child who is abused should not go through life carrying these mental scars.
We need to have rehabilitation for these children. We need counselling for these children. We also have to streamline and modify our court procedure so that these children go through a minimum amount of trauma and the cases are heard as early in the court docket as possible.
Currently judges tell juries that there is a danger in convicting on the uncorroborated evidence of a child. Bill C-126 would repeal this rule and a child's testimony would have the same weight as an adult's, which is a major step forward.
Where an accused represents himself in cases of child sexual assault the judge would now be allowed to appoint counsel for the accused to conduct the cross-examination of the child witness.
Bill C-126 would allow a judge to permit a friend or relative of the child's choice to be close to the child witness while testifying. This is designed to reduce the psychological trauma which these children usually suffer. The support person would be instructed not to communicate with the child while the child is testifying.
Currently a judge can exclude any and all spectators from a court room in the interest of the public morals or the proper administration of justice. Bill C-126 suggests a test be included in the code to strike a better balance between the right of the public to be present and the interest of the child.
Government Orders
These are important. We basically support what is in this legislation. There are some questions of course. Basically the thrust of what the government wants to do is proper and is a step forward. Nevertheless there are some concerns as I have said.
I want to rediscuss a situation in which the accused represents himself in cases of child sexual assault. Now the judge would be allowed to appoint counsel for the accused to conduct a cross-examination of the child witness. That is for a very good reason because the child could be five, six, nine or ten years of age. It could be a trauma for the child to have the person who actually committed the sexual abuse questioning the child, being up close to the child and questioning in a menacing fashion. We are saying if this is going to be problematic for the child witness then somebody else should be appointed.
Should we put some qualifying interests here because of the interests of the accused and on the basic principle of our law that a person is innocent until proven guilty? Should it be a counsel who comes in cold without knowing the case or without knowing the child, without having any feeling for the legal process of what is transpiring in this case and just ask the questions? How is this to be done? If the counsel does this, while it safeguards the child which is certainly what we want psychologically, is the accused jettisoning his or her fundamental right in the case before this court? Will the Supreme Court of Canada allow this if we do not modify it in some way?
These are concerns that I have and I think these are questions which need to be looked at before the legislative committee. I still think we can do this and get the bill back to the House and on to the Senate before the House adjourns.
There are other points that I want to make that are important. The requirement that a victim must reasonably fear for his or her safety could be problematic. Such a test is traditionally known as the reasonable man test. What is reasonable to cause a woman to be afraid? This may be much different from what is reasonable to cause a man fear. Police and judicial training will be critical if this problem is to be overcome. We used to talk about in law and still talk about the reasonable man test. We also

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
have to look at what is genuinely reasonable to cause fear to a woman who is being stalked.
A recent study funded by the Ontario Women's Directorate found that of the 551 women murdered in Ontario between 1974 and 1990, 78 per cent were killed by former spouses or companions who stalked them prior to their deaths. Anyone who says that stalking is a remote occurrence or a figment of some woman's imagination should memorize the statistic that of the 551 women murdered in Ontario between 1974 and 1990, 78 per cent were killed by former spouses or companions who stalked them prior to their deaths. Women's fears are well grounded. One of the challenges remaining is to convince the police, the Crown attorneys and the judiciary that this is the case.
I have a problem, as I mentioned at the outset, with the government's motivation for introducing this bill. With the House sitting for only five more weeks before recessing, we may be able to get this legislation. I hope we can. There is other legislation coming forward today on the Order Paper. There will be two more bills tomorrow and I suspect there will be a child pornography bill next week. There may be amendments to the Young Offenders Act. This is not allowing the time that we should have had to debate these questions. There is no reason in the world why these bills could not have been brought before the House earlier than has been the case.
Evidently the government wants to be able to take credit for introducing this legislation. If it was really serious about these issues it would have done something in the preceding months, not to mention the preceding almost nine years.
As I mentioned to the minister yesterday, the bill in regard to the amendments to the Human Rights Act is also something for which we have been waiting.
What is more important than this bill, even though we are talking about it, is that this bill is an intricate part of what we want to achieve for the safety of women and children. It is a very important part but what we need most of all are attitudinal changes within society.
I have mentioned the concern I have that the police, the Crown attorneys and the judiciary are not going to be sensitized to the fear that women have of being stalked,
of criminal harassment and of the fear and the actual prevalence of the abusive situations that exist for women and children in our society today.
Men particularly must condemn the mind-set which has allowed family violence. Women have been talking about it for years but because men have said: "Men could not do this sort of thing, I would not do this sort of thing," it has been sloughed off.
It is time to stop sloughing off these very real concerns. It is time for men to come forward and demand changes to the law with respect to violence against women and children, to demand and promote a change in the mind-set of people in this country.
As men we must do something. We have seen that women cannot do this alone and if they have to do it alone it is going to take much longer than should be the case. Everyone in Canada is concerned about the increase in crime and violence in our communities.
It has been said that the criminal harassment provisions in this bill may be used against legitimate strikers and protests. With all due respect to those who honestly feel this, and I know they honestly believe it, I am not as concerned about this as some people are.
Section 423 of the Criminal Code adequately looks after this concern. The member for New Westminster- Burnaby has mentioned this and it is a subjective weighing in one's mind whether one feels that this is a real problem or not.
She very rightly brought forward in discussions that some 30 states in the United States have anti-stalking legislation that actually provides for this possibility, that it could be used against strikers or those following through with their legal rights under labour legislation.
There have also been fears expressed that this legislation could be used against women who repeatedly call their ex-husbands for overdue support payments. To me this is a more valid concern. While the government argues that a man receiving such phone calls could not reasonably fear for his safety, the danger is that police will use this same argument against a woman who is receiving unsolicited gifts such as love letters and flowers, which are part of the stalking procedure, to let the woman know that the man is still there and is still obsessed with creating fear in the mind of this woman.
May 6, 1993

Other than extensive police and judicial training, it is going to be very difficult to address this concern legislatively. We must work, as I have said and want to repeat again, on the mind-set of society, in particular those who are charged with enforcing or will be enforcing, we hope, this legislation.
Perhaps some more serious consideration should be given to the suggestions of Quebec coroner Anne-Marie David who investigated two recent stalking-related deaths in that province. What she has suggested bears scrutiny and consideration by all Canadians. She stated: "Court houses and police stations should have information desks reserved for victims of conjugal violence so that they know their rights and can overcome insecurities about pressing criminal charges."
There should be somebody in each major police station in this country to whom a woman can go to press charges of criminal violence or her call can be directed. It should not be somebody who is overworked, who is completely insensitive to the concerns of violence against women and violence against children. It should be somebody who has received proper training. All police should have this training, but until this happens there should be, as Madam David has said, a particular desk, a particular place for these people to go to press charges.
Also, convictions and bail conditions in conjugal violence should be marked with a special code in the police computers to ensure swift action against recidivists. We must know who these people are. Women should be informed when their violent partner is being released from jail or on bail. Suspects ordered to turn over weapons should be accompanied from court by a police officer who seizes the weapons immediately. It should not be left to the individual on his or her honour to turn over the weapons. We should have someone go from the court room to seize these weapons.
Measures should be taken to see men removed from the family home in cases of conjugal violence. We in the Liberal Party have been suggesting this for some time. Why, when a woman is abused and/or her children are abused must she leave with the children, leaving the man in the home where she and the children have lived without any threat to the husband, from where the
Government Orders
children go to school and where the friends of the children are located? Why should this be?
One may say that the husband knows where his wife and children are and can come back and harass them or commit sexual or physical assault on them. If that is the concern of the wife then she has the option to leave. However if the wife wants to stay with the children, why can she not stay in the home with her children? Why can the police not be sensitized to know that this is her right and the right of the children? The abuser could be brought before the courts or a justice of the peace immediately or within hours to get a peace bond, and if that peace bond is violated, to have that violation of the peace bond brought before the courts, not weeks or months later, but hours.
Why can this not be done? Why can justices of the peace not be hired to do this? Why do women and children have to live in fear because our legal system is not prepared to give them the protection they deserve? Why is this happening? Why?
Quebec recently brought forward a public education program whereby women would be advised of the protection they could have if they were abused or felt threatened. So many women came forward for this protection and information that it completely jammed and overloaded the system so it became practically inoperative.
The need is out there. The example in Quebec has proven this. Why can we not do something? Why is the federal government not taking the lead in working with the provinces to address these questions? We need to address these questions.
We have to work with the provinces. I am tired of hearing that this cannot be done because it is a provincial responsibility. Why are women's lives being placed in jeopardy because we live in a country with a federal system of government? That is not good enough. More has to be done and done soon.
I also want to bring out one more point that Madam David made in her suggestions, which was that consideration be given to following the lead of London, Ontario in having a social worker accompany police to scenes of domestic violence. That is an excellent suggestion as well.

Government Orders
This legislation does quite a bit. It is a major step forward but there are a lot of pieces missing. We need to work on the attitudinal problem that exists, particularly with the judiciary, the Crown attorneys and the police. That has to be changed. Things have to be done faster.
We know that men who criminally harass women, who abuse women, who abuse children, are not going to stop. We cannot say that because we do not have the finances it is somebody else's jurisdiction. We cannot continue to say that this cannot be done. It has to be done. It has to be done soon. The longer we take, the more women are going to be murdered by husbands, former husbands, boyfriends, lovers and in many cases just men who have been infatuated with them over the years. Over the years they have undergone this trauma.
The provinces seem to be doing more. Some of what they are doing is impressive. With a concerted program initiated by the federal Department of Justice, by the Minister of Justice, a lot more can be done. I do not want to go over what has not been done in the past. I think I have said that.
That is not going to bring back any of the women who have been murdered. It is not going to repair the physical and psychological damage to women who have been sexually assaulted and who have been beaten by their husbands or other men. It is not going to erase the trauma from children's minds which they will be carrying around perhaps for the rest of their lives. By doing something we can stop this in a more committed and meaningful way from happening to others in our society.
Ontario has found some very interesting statistics recently. According to a government survey released just a few days ago 49 per cent of those asked believe women provoke sexual assault with their clothing or behaviour. Even today 49 per cent of the people in a survey believe that women actually bring on their own assaults.
If that does not speak volumes about the need for attitudinal change, education in our schools and a public program to educate our society, I do not know what does.
We talk about wanting to do something about violence against children. A psychiatrist spoke recently before the
Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General during a hearing on crime prevention. He said that if we want to make the most meaningful impact on children so they do not become children at risk and young offenders then the best time to work with them is between the day they are bom and their third birthday. The younger we identify potential children at risk, the more we can do to help them.
Our school system is important, yet there are people who say that is a provincial jurisdiction. Let us work with the provinces. Do not do it without the provinces. After all, the federal government has promoted the Canada food guide. Surely we can do something to actually reduce child sexual abuse and violence in the home.
Another statistic says that 66 per cent of those people polled believe drug or alcohol consumption is a major cause of sexual assault. That maybe true in a lot of cases, but we cannot allow that to become something we use to postpone dealing with the problem. That is like saying automobile accidents are caused because of over-consumption of alcohol.
I also want to commend the province of Quebec for the work it is doing. I want to read a statement from May 5 of this year. It says:
Deadbeat dads who don't keep up with child support payments may lose their driver's licence and have their income tax refund seized, warns Quebec's justice minister. Gil Remillard says he plans to introduce a bill this autumn to make it easier to collect support payments. "The question of support payments is of deep concern because it affects the greatest problem of women heading singleparent families," Remillard told a legislative committee Monday. Support payments are not a way of punishing a wage-earning spouse after a marriage breakup, he said. "They are a parental obligation".
There are signs that things are improving.
I want to work with the government to get this legislation through. We want to examine it. We want to deal with it constructively. Let us move on and do more to correct the problem of abuse against women and children in this country.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to speak on Bill C-126 which is a proposed piece of legislation which would criminalize the ongoing harassment and terrorism particularly of women by ex-partners or by strangers.
May 6, 1993

I want to give some examples of what kind of behaviour we are talking about today. Many people have shared their horrific experiences with me. A woman is confined and sexually assaulted for nine and a half hours. Her attacker's trial is in three months' time and he is out on bail. He is terrorizing her, stalking her and trying to intimidate her into not testifying. She has called the police. They say they cannot do anything. She got a restraining order which he broke and he received only 15 months of probation. He is still out there following her, threatening her and her children.
Another man developed an obsessive interest in a woman he did not know after seeing her in a restaurant. This young woman lives in my community in British Columbia. For four years he has phoned her at work and at home at all hours of the day and night, up to 20 calls a day. He has sent her letters, followed her on the street and watched her house at night. He has insisted he is going to marry her. He has damaged her car and phoned her to call her names which I cannot repeat here. This woman has had to move from her home and get an unlisted phone number. She has contacted the police.
The offender has admitted all of his actions to the police but no charges were laid. Police said that what he had done was not a crime. She also got a restraining order but it was completely ineffective and continues to be.
Probably the most common case of stalking is when a woman is terrorized by an estranged husband or boyfriend. In one case a woman suffered physical and psychological abuse by her partner for seven years. She left him, which takes great courage, and he refused to accept that she was taking control over her own life. He has been stalking her for three years now. He watches her home and her work place. He follows her to stores and to the homes of friends. She has received over 300 calls from him in four months. She is afraid to go outside. She has contacted the police but they did not lay charges. They told her that unless he threatened her directly or physically harmed her they could not do anything.
The abusive behaviour continued to escalate and then they did lay charges. She now has a court order that says he cannot contact her, follow her, watch her or come within 500 metres of her work place or home. He has
Government Orders
broken all of these restrictions and yet only one charge has been laid. He received a $300 fine and two years of probation but no jail term. He continued to stalk her.
In court his lawyer tried to make a case that she really wanted his advances and was playing hard to get. She has no privacy. Her children worry about her safety. He has pointed a gun at her neighbour and tried to force a man who he thought she was dating off the road. He has told her he will fix it so she can never have a relationship with another man and no man will ever want to date her.
Imagine having to live like this for the rest of one's life. Imagine having to live with one's curtains drawn, afraid that someone is peering in one's window. Imagine being afraid to answer the phone, afraid of a stream of abusive language, threats or just plain silence. Imagine being afraid to leave one's home or afraid to come back to one's own home.
These are just a few of the actual cases I have received from women who have been stalked and who gave me permission to use their stories as examples of what we are talking about today.
Too often women are killed by those who have stalked them. The majority of women who are murdered in Canada are murdered by their partner or ex-partner. Often this type of criminal harassment or terrorism has been a precursor to that murder.
In all the cases I have given we are talking about power and control, or the attempt to have power and control over another person's life. It really has nothing to do with love, affection or spumed love. It is all about power and control over another's life.
Unfortunately, some police officers, some Crown attorneys and some judges do not see this behaviour as threatening, or they feel they do not have the tools to do anything about it. Recent hearings before the commission on policing in British Columbia have confirmed what women's organizations and women who have been stalked have known for a long time: restraining orders do not work.
In one municipality police say they will not enforce restraining orders at all because they call for a peace officer to enforce them and they do not consider the orders specific enough. Police across the province say they are reluctant to enforce restraining orders because

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
they do not know whether or not the order has been varied by the same or another judge.
Restraining orders leave the onus on the woman. Getting a restraining order requires a woman to go to court. She must pay for lawyers and must wait while her life may be at risk. We certainly need to reform the code provisions to enable the police to react right away to criminal harassment without leaving the onus on these terrorized women themselves.
What is required is not only a law but mandatory education for the judiciary and law enforcement officials in how and when to use it. They need to have in-depth training about violence against women and women's equality. They need to be able to see these events from the perspective of a woman who has been abused and terrorized. Otherwise the law will be meaningless.
One of the concerns I have raised with the bill, and I know others have, is the issue of reasonable fear. Police officers, Crown attorneys and judges will have to accept that the harassment was enough to cause fear in a reasonable person.
Who is this reasonable person? The Minister of Justice has assured me that the woman's circumstances will be taken into account. How can he assure me of that when every day police are called and some are aware of women's circumstances but some certainly are not?
Is the reasonable person someone leading a relatively privileged life with a lot of power and faith in the system, who has the money to take steps to protect herself? That is likely the person who will be deciding whether or not to pursue the charges in court. The panel on violence against women heard from one lawyer who said that when a battered woman comes to him he usually tells her to go back to her husband because she will probably end up there anyway.
Does this man understand what an abused woman's reasonable fear is? Is the judge who makes the final decision about whether a woman reasonably feared for her life and safety well versed in how abuse and harassment affect women's lives? There is no mandatory training or screening of judges or Crown prosecutors on these issues before or after they are appointed to the
bench. That is what must go hand in hand with this legislation.
I want to make it clear that there are police officers, Crown attorneys and judges out there who are compassionate and who have acted in the best interests of women. However we are all familiar and we all know of cases where the most inappropriate comments about women's lives have come from the bench itself.
All of them, not just some of them, need to have the information about the effects of violence against women, including criminal harassment which will help them do their jobs effectively and act quickly to prevent the abuse and deaths which result from this behaviour.
Some people have advised women who are harassed and stalked to quit their jobs, pull their children out of school and move away but moving often does not solve this problem. These men are obsessed with controlling these women's lives. Short jail terms do not appear to deter them. They continue their harassment and follow these women to other provinces and even other countries.
Women cannot afford to hire private security guards and why should they? Why should victims of a crime be the ones to pay?
I am interested in seeing a strong and effective anti-stalking law which will be properly enforced. I congratulate the Minister of Justice on bringing this bill forward. I only wish, as the previous speaker said, we had seen it earlier.
It is in this interest that I hope the government will agree to hold full committee hearings and be flexible about accepting amendments which will strengthen the bill. I have outlined my concerns about the bill in a letter to the Minister of Justice and he replied. I know he also would like to see this bill passed quickly.
We must ensure the bill reflects the realities and concerns of women who have been stalked and the women who have raised our awareness about the issues of violence against women. I want to see the bill clarified, particularly the reasonable fear aspect, and I want to see a clause that does exempt legitimate labour disputes.
May 6, 1993

Two of the minister's officials have said that the bill could not be used in labour disputes. One of them said it probably could be used in a labour dispute, and it should be, if picketers exhibited the behaviour described in the bill. This shows a lack of understanding of the ongoing terror women face at the hands of abusive men who stalk them in comparing them with labour picketing. It also shows an absolute faith in the criminal justice system which is not borne out by history.
I appreciate the minister's point that section 423 is rarely used in labour disputes so there is little likelihood that this stalking provision will be used for that purpose, but we must not enact Criminal Code provisions which could capture behaviour we do not want to see captured.
Sexual assault laws were not designed to punish people who have AIDS, but they have twice been used to charge people who may have transmitted the AIDS virus to others. The criminal harassment provision of Bill C-126 is based on wording similar to a statute specifically designed to be used in labour disputes.
If the government does not intend the bill to be used this way, it should adopt just such a proviso as some of the bills in the United States have exempting legal labour picketing, as my private member's bill did. I understand the minister does not want to make exceptions for some circumstances and not others, but there is a precedent for such exemptions within the Criminal Code of Canada.
Homicide is against the law but in the circumstances of self-defence it is not punished as murder. There are laws on the books about sedition, with an exception for peaceful criticism of the state. There are exceptions in firearms laws for members of the Canadian forces and for police officers. It does make sense to include appropriate exemptions in the Criminal Code of Canada as we have done with other legislation.
I would like the government to consider a minimum jail term for people who continue to criminally harass their victims while subject to a restraining order. The minister wrote that this might be too onerous a sentence for someone who disobeyed a restraining order in a minor way and may lead to offences where there is no restraining order in place being taken less seriously.
Government Orders
There is a six-month minimum jail term for a second offence of drunk driving. It is meant to communicate that government takes the issue of drunk driving seriously. Stricter drunk driving laws and education on this issue have resulted in a change in societal attitudes about driving while impaired and subsequently a decrease in this kind of dangerous behaviour.
Surely the government must treat violence against women equally seriously. Lives and health are just as much at risk. We cannot overnight change abusive men and social attitudes which allow this kind of abuse against women to continue. A criminal harassment law will not stop criminal harassment altogether, but we can get abusive men away from their victims while we continue to work every day on the larger issues that are the root cause of violence against women. I do not believe that six months in jail is too onerous a sentence for a repeat offender.
I maintain my concern that two similar provisions will exist in the Criminal Code but with very different penalties. Why is it that following with intent to harass carries a maximum penalty of five years but following with the intent to control someone's lawful movements and behaviour is punishable only on a much lesser penalty of summary conviction?
Stalkers are trying to control the lives, the movements and the behaviour of their victims. In some cases the wording of existing section 423 can better apply to the situation of stalking, and yet police officers are supposed to somehow magically know they are not supposed to use that section. Some police officers currently charge stalkers using section 423. It is simply inappropriate to have essentially the same behaviour criminalized twice with substantially different penalties. The portions of section 423 which overlap with this new provision should be repealed.
The minister said in his letter to me that there was virtually no overlap between the two provisions and that they differed quite markedly. I would like to read into the record subsection 423(1) with paragraphs (c) and (f), and then I will read the proposed criminal harassment provision with paragraphs (a) and (c).
Everyone who wrongfully and without lawful authority, for the
purpose of compelling another person to abstain from doing anything
that he has a lawful right to do, or to do anything that he has a lawful

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
right to abstain from doing, persistently follows that person from place to place, or besets or watches the dwelling-house or place where that person resides, works, carries on business or happens to be.
The new provision states:
No person shall, without lawful authority and with intent to harass another person or recklessly as to whether the other person is harassed, engage in conduct referred to subsection (2) that causes the other person reasonably to fear for their safety or the safety of anyone known to them. The conduct consists of repeatedly following from place to place the other person or anyone known to them, or besetting or watching the dwelling-house, or place where the other person, or anyone known to them, resides, works, carries on business or happens to be.
There are differences, and in many ways the new wording is better in that the element of recklessly as to whether harassment occurs means that intent to harass does not have to be proven. The new provision is broader in that if a woman's children or other family members are stalked this would also constitute a part of the harassment behaviour. However there are also similarities and this leaves the situation unclear.
What is the definition of communicating when it is used in the bill? Does it include sending flowers every day, putting flowers inside a locked car so the woman would know that he could get to her at any time? Does it include putting a cup with the logo of her work place on her doorstep at home to let her know that he knows where she is working?
The minister has assured me this would probably be seen as communicating, but I am not sure probably is good enough. There are provisions in the Criminal Code that police could now use to charge stalkers but they are not consistently used. Women have faced some appalling attitudes within the criminal justice system.
We have to spell provisions out for many people. We cannot assume that the police and the justice system personnel are telepathic or understand exactly what the minister means in the legislation. We must make the law as clear as possible and as reflective as possible of women's own experiences of dealing with this kind of terrorizing behaviour.
There is a lot of non-verbal stuff that goes on. Leaving dead rats on the doorstep, is that communicating? Why should Crown attorneys have to focus on whether such an act constitutes communication instead of criminalizing any act meant to harass, alarm or frighten an
individual? We must give the police the tools they need to charge these individuals and not make it difficult for police and Crown attorneys to use the law and put them in a position of having to second guess what Parliament's intent is.
The minister argued against broadening the law past communication because non-criminal types of behaviour could be caught, but the law clearly states that there must be an intent to harass. It should not matter how that harassment manifests itself. If an act is meant to harass and cause fear in the victim, that should be good enough to exclude any innocuous behaviour. The restrictive definition in the bill may exclude many of the behaviours actual stalkers use to intimidate, to frighten and to control their victims' lives.
Some 26 B.C. municipalities have so far passed resolutions in favour of anti-stalking legislation. I want to co-operate with the government in supporting this bill as long as adequate consultation with concerned groups takes place and the government is flexible about amendments that will strengthen the bill.
The bill also contains provisions unrelated to criminal harassment that would make it easier for child witnesses to testify in court. It would prevent repeat paedophilic sex offenders from holding positions of trust over children or from loitering around schools and playgrounds. I support these provisions. This represents a humane understanding of the reality of child sexual abuse and these are sensitive steps to change procedures of court testimony for children.
The bill would also overturn existing law stating that a wife and husband cannot be accused of conspiring with each other. This law was put in place when the husband and wife were seen as one person, the husband, and reflects sexist attitudes. I feel we should be moving in a direction that recognizes women as free and independent individuals.
However the concerns I have about the lack of adequate mandatory education for police officers, Crown attorneys and judges in issues of violence against women and women's equality may lead to charges of conspiracy being brought against women who have been coerced into whatever behaviour simply by the fact that she is in an abusive relationship. The courts do not have a
May 6, 1993

consistent and adequate grasp of the inequality of power and dynamics of abuse within marriages.
In conclusion, mandatory, in-depth education must come hand in hand with changes in laws so that police forces, Crown prosecutors and judges understand the reality of this kind of behaviour, and the social and economic power differences between men and women in our society.
I support this bill as a positive first step by the Minister of Justice. I hope very sincerely that we can do the work that needs to be done in the committee stage to ensure that this bill passes, with amendments, before Parliament adjourns.

Madam Speaker, I have a comment and a question.
First of all, I would like to congratulate the member for New Westminster-Burnaby on a very powerful, detailed and persuasive speech. I see the Minister of Justice in the House and I am pleased about that. I am sure he was listening.
This is a model of how we should be doing legislation. I know the member for New Westminster-Burnaby mentioned in her speech that she had exchanged letters with the minister and some detailed responses about how to make this bill better. I want to express my view, as the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby did, that the minister should seriously consider, and I think he said yesterday in the justice committee he would, the changes that we in the New Democratic Party have suggested would make this stalking bill more effective.
The member for New Westminster-Burnaby mentioned the appalling attitudes in the criminal justice system. She said that the law should reflect women's experiences and detailed a number of experiences and specific situations. I started in the criminal justice system, believe it or not about 20 years ago now, as a young Crown attorney. My boss was a fellow named George Campbell.
I thought you were going to say as an offender.

No, not as an offender. My first job was as a Crown attorney in the family court. My boss was a fellow named George Campbell who had two daughters, one of whom is running for the Conservative leadership.
Government Orders
I recall our attitudes at the time, those of all of us, not just the prosecutors. It was a good group of people. We worked with the police and they were good. However sometimes our attitudes lingered from another era. The attitude was that the woman said she was threatened but she has said that before and she will be back with him so let us get a restraining order. If there was a case in which we thought that a woman was going to be hurt we would do our best to get a restraining order.
However, it was true in those days and I think it is still true, as the hon. member said forcefully, that restraining orders are weird things in the justice system. They vary, are not obeyed enough, are difficult for the police and so on. I thought she made a good point. It was borne out in my own personal experience, albeit a few years ago, in the criminal justice system as both a Crown attorney and defence counsel. I know my attitudes have had to change a lot, helped I might say by the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby.
Could the member tell the House a little bit more about her own private members' bill, how it differed from the government's bill and how she came about presenting the bill? I know she was ahead of the government on this issue. She has been leading the country on this issue.
This is perhaps an odd question but I think I can ask it in the tone of this debate. I was particularly impressed, and I think some of the members listening in the House were impressed, by the examples that the hon. member kept mentioning.
There was the rat at the door, the flowers in the car, the continual harassment. He even said he would go to another country or she would never have an affair with another man, or stopping the other man's car when he thought she was having a relationship with him when she was not.
Where did she get all these examples? Are women coming to her and saying these things? I would like to know a little more about that. I suspect some of the people who are watching on television and the people in the House would be interested.

Madam Speaker, I thank my colleague from Port Moody-Coquitlam for his comments and his role as justice critic in our caucus, which he performs so well.

He helps me with the work that I am doing in terms of justice for women.
He asked where my bill came from. My own private member's bill that I introduced a few months ago came from the examples that I gave in my speech.
These are women who have contacted me and told me the tragedy and harassment they have been undergoing in situations of this kind of stalking.
