We should all remember that decades ago these groups were advocating and bringing forward the issues of violence against women.
They raised our consciousness about that issue and have been the ones who have been providing support for terrorized women in these kinds of situations. It has not been our society in any structural way but the grassroots organizations formed by women and supported by women that have offered the support to battered women and women in situations of crisis in their lives.
I think we should all acknowledge their courage and the courage of the women who have told their stories that have resulted in this legislation coming forward.

Madam Speaker, I have one other comment about another matter, in the spirit of this open debate we are having in the House.
In my speech I want to talk about reasonable fear because I am not sure I actually agree with the hon. member on that. Maybe it is because I think as a criminal lawyer. I am going to debate that a little bit more.
One of the points I wanted to raise was her raising the impaired driving case. I want to tell her in the House that I think it is a perfect example. I can remember when I was a prosecutor and a defence counsel. The attitude was that impaired driving was an offence, but boys will be boys or people will nudge, nudge, wink, wink. After we look at the statistics of the deaths and the difficulties, now it is much more serious.
Young people will now say: "You better not get in the car, Dad" or "You better be careful there, friend." We can see the difference. It came about by a public campaign and tougher penalties. That mandatory jail term did have an effect.
I just want to second what the hon. member said. I see parallels to that in what is happening with the threatening legislation and translated in the stalking. It was never really treated as being serious. Where there is a public component, as the hon. member mentioned in her speech, the educational component, we have to go with the two. The fellow who keeps harassing that woman and will not obey the threat of it then has to get hit hard and go to jail. There also has to be education generally. I think we are on that path, thanks to a large extent to the hon. member's work and I will not ask her to reply to that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Minister of Western Economic Diversification and Minister of State (Environment) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to participate for a few minutes in this very important debate. I was delighted to hear both the Minister of Justice and the members of the two opposition parties giving their support in principle to Bill C-126 which is before us and to indicate that hopefully we can move ahead through the committee and have this bill come into law before this House recesses for the summer.
May 6, 1993

That is an indication of the co-operative nature of this House on some of these important issues, on something the Canadian public really wants. We can come together around issues that are important for Canadians, in this case the women of Canada, and take measures that are going to be of help to them.
This bill covers a variety of issues. The stalking issue is the issue that most of us have been addressing in this debate, but I do not think we want to forget that there are issues in this bill that relate to the protection of children and other components that relate to the protection of women. I think particularly of the provision that would enable a woman to leave her family home and take her children with her if she was a victim of violence and not be in any fear of the law saying she was abducting those children. That is important.
There is also the provision under which it would be a crime to take a child out of the country for the purposes of an activity that would be illegal in Canada. That has been an issue that has certainly come to my attention, particularly with respect to female castration and sexual offences against children. Those are two other areas that are very important in this bill.
I do want to come back to the provisions that relate specifically to criminal harassment, which is commonly known in the press as stalking. It is interesting that we are dealing with this issue.
I want to pay credit to the women of this House, the women on all sides of the House, who have made a remarkable difference. When I go out and talk to women I talk about how we must have more women in Parliament to bring their views, get involved in the public policy process and the making of laws because we do bring a different experience.
What has also been important, which was mentioned by my colleague and others, is that the awareness of these issues by our male colleagues has really become quite profound. I have noticed a remarkable change in terms of understanding because there has been this kind of interaction. That has to be all to the good for the Canadian public.
We now have a law in front of us that has come to this House as a result of a lot of work. I am sure that even five years ago people would not have been talking about this. It was happening. It was certainly happening to women, but there was a feeling that it was not on the public agenda. There was that provision in the Criminal Code which might have been used in certain circum-
Govemment Orders
stances. Women's organizations and individual women have brought this issue forward, as have women in the political areas both here in this House and at the provincial level. Many of my colleagues, status of women ministers at the provincial levels, have also raised this issue with me.
As a result of that we were able to come forward now, actually very quickly because the minister is just a new minister. His predecessor was certainly seized of this issue. We had communicated and discussed it on a number of occasions. The new minister has come forward and very quickly moved ahead with the conference in Toronto, to listen to the concerns that are coming forward and to introduce this legislation at this point.
It has been discussed certainly in earlier speeches of why the legislation is important. The statistics show that 48 per cent of women who are murdered are murdered by either husbands or ex-partners. We do not know exactly how many of those women may have been stalked or harassed. Even if it is only one or two, it is important that we have provisions in our law that might avoid those tragedies, might help them be able to live their lives without the fear of violence.
We certainly know the individual case studies of women who have been the victims of this kind of harassment in all its variations, whether it is the person who telephones constantly using threats, or besets, watches outside or drives by. We have heard a lot of it. Just recently in British Columbia there were a number of cases and more recently in Manitoba three very tragic cases.
We all know this kind of behaviour occurs. Sometimes people will ask: how does this happen in a society like ours? It is hard to know what goes on in the minds of those who stalk. It is not acceptable. It is certainly one part of dealing with the whole issue of how we can eliminate violence against women in our society, how we can ensure that women can live full equal lives in Canadian society. This is one part, one piece of putting together that full puzzle.
When I talked with the co-chairs of the Canadian Panel on Violence Against Women they certainly raised this issue with me as well. I am looking forward to their report because I think it is going to really help us develop a more holistic view of many of the issues and the underlying attitudes and assumptions which need to be

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
changed in our society to deal with the broader issue of violence against women.
We are today dealing with one part of that puzzle. I was pleased to hear some of the specific issues that have been raised. I know in committee they will get an opportunity to look into them. As I look at this bill I see very important advantages in setting out very clearly the tests that are required under this bill. I think they are tests that are really important to women.
First of all, in our legal system there has to be the premise that one is innocent until proven guilty, and there would have to be an appropriate test. However this one says okay, there is either the intent to harass or there is recklessness in the behaviour or the conduct which then leads to harassment. There are the two elements there that are important.
The most important element is that it is the victim, primarily women although not exclusively, who then has a fear for her safety or the safety of her family. It is her view, it is her fear that is the test. I am not a lawyer but as I understand it after talking with lawyers that is the important point here. It is not someone else's test of reasonableness, it is because of her own experience, her own view. That is the test. In my mind that is one of the most important advances in this bill over some of the other pieces of legislation that I have seen even in the United States. We have certainly looked at those and tried to find through their experience what kind of improvements we might be able to include. I see this as an important move forward in that respect.
In terms of the description of the kinds of conduct, certainly it illustrates for us the besetting and the watching. In the provision that deals with communicating, it is communicating both directly or indirectly so that it can encompass the whole range of the kinds of activities which were mentioned before in this House. It might be sending flowers. We all like to receive flowers. But if one was sending flowers in a way and as a result of a history that would lead the woman to fear for her safety then that could be conduct which could be included as criminal harassment. Obviously each case would be looked at on its own merit.
As we examine the provisions of this bill we see they really are a remarkable move forward in providing not
only to women but also to the police the tools that they need in order to lay charges for this kind of activity.
I had the opportunity on Sunday to participate in a television show on Newsworld on this issue with phone-in calls. One of the calls came from a policewoman named Susan in Vancouver. She said just how important she felt this legislation was going to be to her as a policewoman to enable her to deal with situations, to give her the legal tools to be able to lay charges in those kinds of situations. She applauded this bill and remarked what an important move forward it is.
It is going to be a help there. It is going to be a help within our justice system, obviously, both for the lawyers and judges to have this kind of clear definition.
It is also going to be important in terms of the message it sends to society. Obviously legislation not only has a role in punishing those who commit the behaviour but also in preventing it. Ideally what we would like to do is prevent people from criminally harassing others.
By having a very explicit provision such as this, having very severe penalties with up to five years in jail, that kind of message is going to be out there. It is hopefully going to send a signal to anyone who would think: "Oh well, I can just do this, I can get away with that." It will say no. No, that is not acceptable. You can end up going to jail.
I would hope that would really help us in solving the problem for those to whom this is not a deterrent. Perhaps no law would be a deterrent because of their own behaviour or psychological attitudes. They too will get caught and hopefully removed as a result of jail sentences and no longer able to harass their victims. Those women will be able to live without fear of that kind of activity. This legislation has a lot of components to it that I believe are important.
Colleagues have raised as well the issue where the law is one thing, its implementation is another, and I agree. You have to have a law first obviously. We have to work with all those who are involved in the justice system to ensure that they understand and appreciate the importance of this law and the importance of women's experience.
May 6, 1993

Again I would like to applaud both the current justice minister and his predecessor, the present Minister of National Defence, for the important initiatives they have taken.
The first national conference on women in the justice system which was held in Vancouver a year and a half ago really brought out for the first time in this kind of forum the concerns and the issues. I was part of that meeting. It was a very powerful meeting.
As a result of that, attention is being paid both by ministers responsible for the status of women across the country and attorneys general. We are certainly looking forward to the reports that I anticipate will come forward a little later this spring to help us move forward in dealing with many of those issues.
Work is being done by groups like the Western Canadian Judicial Centre. Justice Campbell who heads up that centre, no relation to my hon. colleague, has really done some ground-breaking work with justices across western Canada in dealing with issues relating to gender in the justice system, aboriginal issues and issues relating to race.
I have attended some of the sessions that have been held, some of the training programs, and they have had a remarkable impact. They have had people almost in tears trying to deal with these very emotional, difficult
issues.
We are seeing important progress. That work has to continue in work through the National Judicial Council as well as being spread throughout other parts of Canada and work with police.
My hon. colleague, the Solicitor General, was here earlier in the House. I have talked with him about the RCMP and the work that is needed. A few months ago I wrote to police chiefs across the country on issues related to how they deal with some aspects of violence against women.
I have been encouraged by the replies I have been getting. There is a great deal of willingness out there. Obviously they need the tools and the programs to assist them.
Government Orders
I am heartened when I hear from police officers such as Susan in Vancouver who obviously understand. They are quite excited by the opportunity of this kind of change in the law.
I would encourage all colleagues, as they go through the hearing process over the next few weeks, to deal with the substance of this bill. If there are improvements that can be made, I know that my hon. colleague will be prepared to look at them and to move forward so that we can get this law into effect. It will help to provide the kind of protection, the legal foundation and the societal message to help us all deal with this and to end violence against women in this society.

Madam Speaker, I listened very carefully to the minister for the status of women. I know that her comments and the comments of my colleague from Halifax today in many ways are going in the same direction but there are a few differences.
The minister mentioned in her speech today about the need for education. She spoke about the voluntary program that has been put in place by the judiciary in British Columbia on gender sensitivity education.
I want to ask her this today. Does she not understand, as I do, that people going to a voluntary program are those who perhaps are the least in need of that kind of gender sensitivity education? Those who do not attend when it is a voluntary program are likely to be the people who are most in need of gender sensitivity education around the issues of abuse of women, power relationships and violence against women. We have all read the outrageous statements made by judges in virtually every jurisdiction in this country about women's reality. They do not think they have a problem. They think their attitude is the societally acceptable attitude.
Would she push her colleagues for mandatory gender sensitivity education for judges, for Crown prosecutors and for police forces so we can have some assurance that these police officers, these judges, these Crown prosecutors most in need of that education will receive it? Then we can go some way to changing the kind of societal attitudes these folks grow up with which are so damaging and allow the revictimization of women to happen within our court system.

May 6, 1993
Government Orders

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Environment)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will try to answer that briefly. Fortunately, those attitudes are changing and it is coming about because of public pressure and because it is not acceptable. Those issues get raised in the newspapers and it creates that kind of pressure.
I have had a lot of discussion about this issue with Justice Campbell and some others about the best way of bringing this about. The sense I still have is that they feel it is more successful than forcing people to do it. The feeling is that their minds will be closed and that they will not be as receptive.
The sense is that the way they are going about it now through the Western Canadian Judicial Centre and the work they are doing is having the greatest impact. They are bringing people into these programs who certainly have not been all that sympathetic to the issues.
That they are there as volunteers, although I think there is a great deal of pressure being put on in a variety of ways for them to go, results in changes of attitudes. The sense is that if we force people to attend there would be quite a backlash. I sensed that one time when I was at another kind of a program.
I think that we should continue to try and do it this way. I am prepared to look at the results of how we are doing. We are making progress, quite substantial progress. In my mind that is the better way to go in this respect.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just briefly, I want to compliment the speakers who have participated in the debate today. In an effort to move things along I am not going to speak, but I hold the views of all of the people who have spoken today. I think some good points have been made.
I would like to address, if I may, the mandatory aspect of the comments of the speaker representing the New Democratic Party. I share the view of the minister that we are making progress and we have to continue to grind it out. We will never stop insensitive remarks from being made no matter how hard we try. We just have to keep grinding it out.
I had occasion to go to Newfoundland and speak to the Provincial Court Judges Association. I saw two very excellent video tapes that have been prepared by the Canadian Judicial Centre, one on family violence and the other on the sexual abuse of children. Both tapes are being used extensively.
I share the NDP member's sentiments on the need to continue to do it. I just have some hesitation with the mandatory aspect of it, especially with the judges. The first thing the judges are going to say is that we are interfering with judicial independence and they will take it off on that tangent. I do not think that serves our purpose, which is identical, to broaden the base of knowledge and sensitivity. I do not think there is any question that we have to do that. It ought to be mandatory that governments keep pushing them. That is where the mandatory aspects should come in.

Madam Speaker, I am very happy to rise to take part in the debate this morning on what is a very necessary and long-awaited piece of legislation.
I want to compliment my colleague, the hon. Minister Responsible for the Status of Women and my colleague from New Westminster-Burnaby, the New Democratic Party's critic for the status of women, because as frequently happens, at least with the three of us, there are agreements that cross all party lines.
I want to talk a little about specifics. It was a very long time ago when I was in junior high school that I first heard the phrase "peace, order and good government". Lest anybody fears, no I am not about to reopen the constitutional debate. Peace, order and good government is the residual clause of section 91 of the British North America Act and it is the federal residual power.
When I first heard that clause in a civics class in junior high school I remember it had a ring to it and that ring has stayed with me all these many years. It is a peculiarly Canadian phrase. The desire for peace, order and good government is one of the things that makes us, as Canadians, anglophone, francophone or allophone, part of our national fabric and different from other people's national fabric.
However without the kind of legislation that this bill approaches a whole segment in our society does not have access to peace and order, not to say good government. Peace and security for women can be a very scarce commodity.
Before I get into the body of my remarks this morning, I want to comment on the questions and comments made by the two ministers earlier with regard to the question of mandatory training of judges. I have been howling, I hesitate to use that word howling, but it might be the appropriate word, for this very measure since the first
May 6, 1993

time I spoke in this Chamber, which I believe was in 1989.
I respect very much both minister's opinions. I understand their concerns about mandatory training and the freedom of the judiciary and all those things. I practised law for 10 years so I realize how important an independent judiciary is. I also know, Madam Speaker, and I think you and a number of other members of this House know, that there are judges with whom we will never make headway. I know judges and if I were not in the House of Commons I would be afraid to say what I am about to say. I am obviously not going to name names, but I know judges in my age group who do not understand what it is we are talking about. I would be prepared to make a fairly strong wager that most of the members of the legal profession in this House know whereof I speak.
There are judges who will not convict, who have the lowest conviction rates in matters that relate to those which require gender sensitivity. There are judges who will not convict in sexual assault cases unless the evidence is so far beyond the question of reasonable doubt that they would be knocked off the bench if they did not convict. There are some who do not convict even in those cases. There are judges who when faced with the inevitability of conviction will then sentence inappropriately. We all know this and we have all seen it. The point is that 40 per cent of the judges in this country, whether we are talking about those appointed federally or provincially, have not voluntarily taken advantage of the Canadian Judicial Institute's gender sensitivity training.
As my colleague from British Columbia said, 60 per cent have taken the sensitivity training. A number of them, certainly in my own region, are judges I know quite well and I have said to them: you people were not the ones I was worried about. I was not worried about them before they took the sensitivity training and I am not worried about them now.
While I do not disagree with the Solicitor General on the question of judicial independence, I am a lot more worried about the peace and security issue for women. While we have judges who still refuse to understand what the situation is then women in this country will not be secure, even when we have this legislation coming in
Government Orders
that, on the face of it, is not too bad. It needs some improvements.
My hon. colleague, the member for Cape Breton- The Sydneys, mentioned in his remarks how he wants to see this get to legislative committee because we think there are things that can improve it. We support the basic spirit, particularly in the area of stalking. We want to see the legislation passed and we want to see it out there. This legislation does not exist in a vacuum. There is only so much we can do as legislators, but there is a lot that the federal government can do by bringing its influence to bear.
I know that the Solicitor General is sympathetic and supportive in these areas. Let me give one anecdote about the RCMP in my constituency. It is actually Dartmouth constituency, but who is counting. I received a call not long ago from a former client and she said: "I do not know who else to call." She had been my client and I had done a divorce and some other work for her over the years.
She was involved in a new relationship and had been co-habiting with this man for six months. On the night in question he became violent. He physically abused her. He hit her. She phoned the police who came. He had already left the house. She said if he came bach she wanted the police to come and remove him from the house. It was her house. She owned the house and in the old Anglo-Saxon term, in fee simple, it was hers. She was the sole owner.
This man had been co-habiting with her for six months. In Nova Scotia the laws relating to matrimonial property only apply to people who are legally married; they do not apply to people who co-habit. TTie RCMP officer told my former client that it was the policy of the RCMP not to remove any man from a house if he had lived there for six months because he suddenly had a right under the Matrimonial Property Act. She said this to me and I told her that was insane.
The RCMP is perpetrating something that does not uphold the law in Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia it is only for people who are married. Whether that is right or wrong does not come into it; that is the law. There was the RCMP telling this woman it could not do anything. One presumes if a total stranger came up and walked into her house the RCMP would come and remove him,

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
but because this guy had lived there for six months it would not remove him.
I called the RCMP detachment and informed the superintendent of the law.
He said that was its policy and I said it was in conflict with the law. He did not think so. I asked for his fax number to fax him the relevant law and he said: "Oh, that doesn't matter."
"Agree with me," I say to the hon. President of the Treasuiy Board. I know he does. This is a case for a little gender sensitivity. We know it is. The point is that this kind of attitude exists. It may not be rampant any more. I do not believe it is rampant any more, but it exists in a significant enough number of cases in police departments. It also exists in Crown offices and, Heaven knows, it exists in the judiciary.
How are we going to eradicate it? I appreciate the minister's comment. I appreciate the Solicitor General's comment that it is easier to bring people through by drawing them in. What is the old expression? You catch more flies with honey than you do with vinegar. The point is that we are losing some of these flies, and women and children are suffering as a result.
We have to do something and that is mandatory training of judges. Those of us in this House can push for mandatory training of judges appointed at the federal level and this government, the Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General can push their provincial counterparts for the same. Women deserve no less. Judges are not gods. They are ordinary mortals. Some of them are excessively ordinary and therefore deserve to be given a chance to understand what is really happening out there. It is for their own good as well as for the common good.
To get to my mutton, although I am not sure how much time I have left, the bill creates a new criminal offence of criminal harassment, what we have long known as stalking. The proposed provision prohibits anyone from repeatedly communicating with or following another person, any member of that person's family or anyone known to that person. It would include persistently following someone, spending extended periods of time watching someone's home or place of work, making harassing telephone calls, making contact with one's friends, neighbours, co-workers, et cetera.
A previous section of the Criminal Code, section 423, prohibited intimidation, but the need for the new law
arose from the difficult burden of proof under that section. Consequently there is good news and bad news in the bill and this is no condemnation of the government. This is the difficulty in passing legislation in this area. It becomes the question of the evidentiary test. The test is that the victim feels fear.
When I was in law school, particularly on the civil side, I can remember a wonderful law professor, a former dean of Dalhousie law school and former vice-president of Dalhousie, Horace Read, standing at the front of the room-I was in his 50th first-year law class-and asking: "What would a reasonable man do in this case?" Then he would say: "Oh, excuse me, what would a reasonable person do?"
In law schools across every country that follows the common law tradition the reasonable man test has always been brought in on the civil side in the area of intentional torts, negligence, et cetera, but it has also been brought in from time to time on the criminal side. The common phrase is: "What would the man on the Clapham omnibus think in this situation?" The problem that worries me, and this is why I want us to look at it very carefully in committee, is whether there is a difference in interpretation as to what the reasonable man would think in the circumstances and what the reasonable woman would think in the circumstances, and whether that particular gender differentiation makes a difference in Crown prosecutors' offices when the time comes to lay an information against an alleged perpetrator. That is my worry. One of the difficulties in communication between men and women in a whole lot of areas is a lack of comprehension about what causes fear.
I raise another anecdote from my law school days. I was taking a criminology course in my final year with three women and eight men. It was a seminar class with a male professor. We were talking about women's fear of violence. When I walked out of Dalhousie law school on University Avenue in the centre of Halifax after dark-it is dark from December until March by 4.30 in the afternoon-I would go to my car, unlock the door, reach in, turn on the dome light, check the back seat, jump in the car and lock the doors. The other two women in the room nodded. They knew exactly what I meant. I suspect that every woman in here knows what I mean as well. It is just something we do. It is one of those things that women do out of self-preservation when they are going to a locked car in the dark.
May 6, 1993

As I said, there were eight men in my class. One was a very dear friend of mine who practises law now in St. John's, Newfoundland. He took it as a personal affront. We argued for the next 40 minutes in class and he considered this to be a totally pointless exercise. He just could not believe that I felt that way or that I thought that way. We argued all the way down five floors in the elevator and out the door of the law school. He walked me to my car. As he was there I did not turn on the dome light or check the back seat. I figured he would check the back seat or he would be in the car. We argued all the way out to dinner and through dinner until I finally dropped him off back at the law school that night.
About six months ago I was in St. John's on political business and I ran into him. He is still arguing with me. This is a man of good faith and with as few gender biases as any male can have. He is of my generation, well educated and all of these things but he still does not see it.
I have argued these points with civil servants, with Crown prosecutors and lawyers and there are still a significant number of men who do not see it. Part of my worry is that if I cannot convince them then I am not quite sure who can.
I know the current Minister of Justice, the previous Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General, the Minister Responsible for the Status of Women, the member for New Westminster-Burnaby, myself and all of us in this House want to ensure that this law will do what it is supposed to do. Therefore it has to have with it the requisite training for those people who are going to be administering and using this law. That means Crown prosecutors, police officers and judges.
If we do not have that training then the scenario will be clear in a number of places. Women will walk in and say: "Buddy has been sitting in his car outside my house for the last three nights." "Did he talk to you?" "No, he did not talk to me." "Has he come near you?" "No, he has not come near me." "Well, what's the problem?" "He frightens me." "Why does he frighten you?" "He just won't leave me alone. He is always there and he
Government Orders
looks at me funny." Believe me I have heard a lot of women, and I am sure many hon. members have too, use the expression: "He looks at me funny." We know what that means and we know that it can create fear.
I am not even faulting men who do not understand it. However I am saying that it exists and that this dichotomy of experience creates a dichotomy of belief. I am very afraid that even with this law and the change that has been long asked for without the requisite gender sensitization for personnel, that woman will leave the Crown office unassisted.
Again we have had the example brought up of flowers. I can hear it. Madam Speaker, I bet you can hear it too. A Crown prosecutor says: "He sent you a dozen roses three days in a row. What are you complaining about?" Yet again, we know what she is complaining about. We know that the arrival of the florist's box strikes terror into her heart. We know that the car parked outside her child's school strikes terror in her heart. The worst thing of all is the frustration of being unable to communicate that terror.
I am not certain that we can amend this legislation. I am not certain that this legislation is not as good as it can be right now. I think that is what committee is for. That is what we have to look at. We have to hear witnesses and do some consultation to know that.
However, I would be prepared at this point to say that this is probably as good as we can do as legislators. However, we have to do more. The government must do more with its influence over the provincial governments and with its own ability to mandate response from its own appointees. That is what we have to do. We have to see this government taking a lead and saying: "You must take these courses if you wish to remain on the bench. You must take these courses if you wish to be the chief personnel officer for the Public Service of Canada so that you understand what sexual harassment is all about. You must take these courses if you are going to be in a position to deal with people who are going to suffer under the disability of being a victim of the kind of behaviour that this legislation has been brought in to combat."

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
If we do not do that then we are offering the women of Canada half a loaf. Half a loaf might be better than none but after all these years and all the suffering, pain and grief the women of Canada deserve better.

Madam Speaker, I just want to make a short comment and offer a suggestion for the consideration of the hon. member, the Minister of Justice, the department and all members of this House.
The bill before us is a very good bill and in fact creates an offence relating to stalking. Inevitably once there is a conviction on that offence there is inevitably going to be a prohibition order issued setting out terms and conditions that would prohibit people from carrying out this kind of activity in the future.
A problem has been pointed out to me by the metropolitan Toronto police department in enforcing that kind of an order. Say a police officer is now called by a past victim who is being protected by this order. When the police officer arrives that person points out the breach of that activity. The police officer then has no power to arrest without a warrant. The police officer has to go away and hopefully return in time to prevent any problem from occurring as a result of a potential breach of that order.
That has two impacts. First, it means that the police officer cannot act immediately in relation to the situation. Second, it creates a lack of confidence in the justice system on the part of the people who are being protected by that order. They see a police officer arrive and then the police officer says he has to leave and that he cannot do anything without going back to a justice of the peace and getting a warrant. He will come back and hopefully the activity will still be going on and he will be able to do something about it.
One may be aware-I believe the Minister of Justice is aware-that I had introduced an amendment on this when we dealt with the Corrections and Conditional Release Act. I put forward my private member's bill, Bill C-393, giving the police officer or peace officer the power to arrest without warrant, where he finds a person breaching a condition of this sort.
The department, I am sure, has some concerns and some problems with that but hopefully we can find a way
to overcome those problems. I would ask that the hon. member, the Minister of Justice and the House give that consideration. It is a very real problem with the enforcement of this kind of legislation once a breach has been established, a conviction has been registered and an order made trying to prevent that from happening in the future.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Don Valley East. As frequently happens I find myself in agreement with his suggestion. I know that the reaction of the police is sometimes very frustrating for the police officers as well because of a lack of the necessary legal tools to deal with a situation such as this.
I am delighted to see that the justice minister is here and perhaps it may be something that we can deal with in committee. Therefore I would certainly support that very strongly if we find that it can make its way into the legislation.
However, I reiterate that is not the only problem. Again I recall another situation that I dealt with in my legal practise. I recall a client calling me one night and telling me that her estranged husband was beating down her back door while she was in her house, very frightened, with her children. I immediately called the police and identified myself. I had been a prosecutor as well as a practising lawyer in private practise and they certainly knew who I was. I reported this incident and told them that there was an order of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia prohibiting this man from coming within* number of feet of his wife's house. The response I got from the police officer was: "How do I know you are a lawyer?" All I wanted to do was drive down to the police station and commit an act of violence myself because the frustration was so bad.
That night the woman fortunately was not hurt but the children in the case saw their father behaving in a manner whereby he broke into the house and there was a violent exchange of words-thank God not blows-in that particular instance. Two small children, not to mention the woman herself, were subjected to a horrific incident because a police officer decided to play cute.
Again many police officers do not react like that. However, while any of them do, we have to do something about the mandatory training.
May 6, 1993

Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure and honour to speak in support of this bill.
Basically this bill will create in particular a new offence of criminal harassment that would prohibit anyone with the intent to harass from repeatedly communicating or following another person, or anyone known to that person. It would also include watching where a person or anyone known to them, lives or works. It would include engaging in threatening conduct directed to that person or any other member of the family. As well this bill would increase the maximum penalty for this offence to five years in prison.
As we know, currently many of the activities usually associated with stalking are covered by the Code but the problem has been that the burden of proof is very high. The victims of stalkers have traditionally had a difficult time convincing police that they had reasonable grounds to fear for their lives.
Only recently in my constituency of Ottawa Centre right in the downtown core of Ottawa we had a very unfortunate incident where one of my constituents who worked in my riding, Patricia Allen, was killed by her estranged husband. We were informed that this individual had carried out threats before and then eventually committed his crime sometime in November 1991.
That is one reason I was delighted to see the government coming forward with this legislation. At least we can prevent those kinds of things from happening in the future to people in our community and our country.
We have seen a trend of increase in violent crimes in our society. In fact, in the city of Ottawa alone for instance, if we look at the statistics from 1991-92, we have an increase in sexual assaults and sexual offences by approximately 43.4 per cent. We also had an increase in assault in general by about 8 per cent. If anything this is a cause for us to be alarmed and to take notice of the grave situation that exists in our community.
A recent study funded by the Ontario Women's Directorate found that of 551 women murdered in Ontario between 1974 and 1990, 78 per cent of those were killed by their former spouses or companions who
Government Orders
stalked them prior to their death. Obviously women's fears are well grounded.
I say this in all fairness because I had an experience in my riding of Ottawa Centre with a constituent of mine just as recently as the beginning of this year, 1993. We dealt with her for a number of months. We tried to help her out while she was going through a very difficult situation.
She had written a letter commenting on her situation, making some suggestions and trying to let parliamentarians and the public know what a woman really had to go through when faced with a situation such as this one. On February 3, 1993 she said: "I laid a complaint against a male adult with the Ottawa police after the person had harassed me at my place of employment over the phone since January 14. Some days I would receive six calls and some days fourteen calls, depending on how drunk he was. On February 2 and 3 he threatened me three times. He threatened to teach me a lesson I would not forget. I should not be stupid. In another call he threatened to take care of me for good and in another he threatened to have his friends take care of me for good. Later that day he told his sister he wanted revenge and he would have the Mafia take care of me. To prove his point a messenger called on his behalf."
Her letter goes on to say that when she informed the police they had a bench warrant issued. The charges were harassment and uttering a threat to do bodily harm. "Two days later, on the advice of the police and my lawyer, I spoke to a justice of the peace and applied for a peace bond. I was told to appear in court three weeks later. If the accused appeared he would be asked to agree to sign the bond. The judge could order the bond or he could be given time to seek legal advice.
This individual was arrested February 11, charged and appeared in court where he was released with an undertaking order. From February 12 to 19 I received calls while he was under that order where the callers hung up when I answered or held on to the line until I hung up or just breathed into the phone.
On my first appearance in the court room I had to wait in the waiting room with this man who had harassed me. This man who had threatened me just walked in off the

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
street and no one searched or checked him. While he did not speak to me he did play with my mind. He glared, he mumbled, he made little gestures, enough to intimidate me into believing he would get me.
I was told a Crown attorney would be available to speak to me prior to the hearing. Well if he or she was there I could not identify him or her." Obviously this constituent has not been to court too often.
"The procedure was" she said, "who was on my side and who was not? What was expected of me? What do I call the judge? I sat for two hours until I realized they used numbers not names. When you are finally called you stand in the aisle as a victim. No one talks to you, they talk around you. You can hardly hear who is speaking, never mind knowing who is speaking.
Defence lawyers, 80 per cent legal aid, and their clients have more rights. They have consulted with each other. You have talked to no one. The case remained for two weeks. No one asked you if it was okay. No one tells you why and the Crown still has not said if they are going to act on your behalf."
Two weeks later this victim went through the same routine. The victim appeared in the court at 8.30 a.m. and this time the accused failed to show. The victim sat in the court room for three and a half hours until the judge ordered a bench warrant. This constituent works and her time is not seen as valuable to the court unfortunately.
She goes on to say: "If I had not appeared at 8.30 a.m. as requested would the court have waited three and a half hours to see if I would appear? No. I expect that if I had failed to appear the case would have been thrown out."
In the meantime this male adult has been unemployed for three and a half years, was given free legal advice, failed to appear and all is okay. Prior to that he had failed to appear on impaired driving. Two weeks later, in early April, he was rearrested, thank God, and received the following charges: an impaired driving charge of 30 days; harassment threats and failing to appear, which were dropped eventually. He was sentenced to only 15 days. The victim was advised of sentencing but not of the release date.
This individual went on to say the following: "As a victim I would die every time the phone rang at work. I would die every time I was paged to go to the main floor of our store. I do not feel safe at home. I do not feel safe at work. I no longer feel I can go for the long walks I used to so much enjoy. I no longer feel I can shop at the Rideau Centre as he used to hang out there. I must always look over my shoulders. I will always be a victim as long as he breathes. I must document everything. I have done everything in my power within the system to handle the situation. If this man wants to carry out his threat he will basically get me one way or another."
I think it is important for the minister to listen to one of those victims and hear what her impression was of the legal system.
She said: "I feel the court system and the officers of the court did not treat this case with the degree of seriousness I feel as a victim. I felt revictimized every time I had to appear in court. I hated being treated like I didn't count or exist. I found the hearings to be confusing, humiliating and overwhelming. I felt I was given the run around."
She went on to say: "I never knew the name of the Crown or whether the person was a male or female and so on. I never knew the name of the judges and I never felt I was given a straight answer from anyone. I couldn't leave the court room during the court time to visit the ladies room for fear while I was out my name would be called and they would think I was a no-show.
I was supposed to be summoned to court after he was rearrested. I'm still waiting, yet I have been to court twice. There was no one to explain your rights or court room procedures. Can I talk unless I am spoken to? Can I ask a question of the court? Can I actually say, 'Sorry, that day and time is not convenient?' I never felt safe in the court room or in the court building."
She goes on. This particular constituent is typical of the many victims all across Canada from coast to coast. I think this bill will go a long way toward dealing with situations such as this.
Of course, there are a lot of improvements needed. Nothing is perfect. At the committee level and the hearing level there are a lot of necessary amendments.
May 6, 1993

Hopefully the government as well as the opposition will co-operate and make sure they are implemented.
There are some points we should note. Court houses and police stations should have information desks reserved especially for victims of violence so they know their rights and can, as this victim did, overcome insecurities about pressing criminal charges.
Convictions and bail conditions, such as in this case should be marked with a special code in the police computer to ensure swift action when repeat offences take place.
Women such as this victim should be informed when their violent partner is being released from jail or is on bail. Suspects ordered to turn over weapons should be accompanied from court by police officers who can seize the weapons immediately. Fortunately in this case, that did not apply but who knows?
Methods should be taken to see men removed from the family house in cases where family violence occurs.
This was part of a proposal that was suggested by our leaders on behalf of the Liberal Party of Canada. Those who are interested in it can call any Liberal member's office to obtain a copy of it.
Consideration should be given to following the London, Ontario lead in having a social worker accompany police to scenes of domestic violence.
These are some of the suggestions and I hope the government will take them to heart when it deals with this legislation to ensure that a proper amendment is made to this bill. Hopefully it will become law before the end of this session in June.
We are concerned on this side of the House that this good piece of legislation will not go through the House of Commons. We want to make sure this legislation becomes law before the end of this term. Otherwise we are back to square one with an election coming, hopefully early this fall.
One would say that the ultimate answer to all this is to go to the root of the problem, to the socio-economic fabric of our society. We must have proper outreach programs for victims as well as potential victims in our society.
Outreach programs should reach out to our educational system through our schools from coast to coast so at
Government Orders
least our youth and our children will be given the necessary information before they finish their schooling and go out into society.
Excellent work has been undertaken by the police force in our city in particular. I have worked with it on a number of occasions and it should be used as a model for police forces across Canada.
Information exchanges should continue. However more important than anything, we must have a co-operative approach when it comes to dealing with the issues of violence, crime prevention and urban safety. We have to have a cohesive approach that goes across municipal, provincial and federal levels.
We have to have a national strategy to deal with the question of urban safety. It is extremely alarming to see the kind of situations that occur on a daily basis, particularly in our urban centres across Canada. I was alarmed by the statistics released lately that showed an increase in violent crimes in this magnificent land of ours.
It showed there has been an increase in the number of irregularities that have taken place in our society. When we compare Canada to the rest of world, we have one of the best and most fascinating social programs anywhere. One would suggest what is lacking perhaps is a strategy to look at the heart and root of the problem itself.
Like any legislation, we have to start moving a little more aggressively in the area of prevention. This legislation is good. It deals with the result of a problem. It deals with a situation after it has occurred, but we also need preventive measures. There is no point giving somebody a pill or medication when perhaps the same problem is going to repeat itself a little later.
I would rather see us focus on ensuring that we have a healthy community and a healthy society through preventive measures. That is where we have to start. The government and society as a whole must try to go to the heart of the problem by introducing proper outreach programs, proper educational programs and proper mechanisms to prevent those kinds of horrible things from happening in our communities and our society.
I want to commend our Ottawa police force for working tirelessly with community groups, non-profit organizations, student and youth organizations, municipal agencies, school boards, business groups and so on. Police organizations such as ours here could and should be used as a model for the rest of the country, for other

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
police forces around Canada and perhaps around the world. I know they are doing a tremendous amount of work in that area. We have to create more partnerships and we have to approach the issue of partnerships in terms of a cohesive approach. I would say there is a lot to be done in this area and we can do a lot more. Obviously this legislation goes a long way in trying to address a good part of the problem, but I can say that no one piece of legislation will solve all the problems all the time. This is a very good step forward.

Madam Speaker, the hon. member mentioned trying to get the bill through before Parliament finishes. We know we are in about the last month of this Parliament. I wanted to take him up on that to see whether he has any proposals.
I do not know if the hon. member is familiar with the fact that today we are debating what we call the stalking bill, Bill C-126.1 think it will pass today as I think there is a feeling of getting it to committee. That means this is second reading and it has to go to committee. It has to come back to the House for third reading and amendments and then it has to go to the Senate to become law.
We are also going to deal with psychoactive substances later today, Bill C-85, which believe it or not, opens up the whole question of marijuana. I cannot believe this government is opening up penalties and dealing with the Narcotic Control Act which would enable some parts of the house to force a vote on that and have the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Defence vote on it. That would be an interesting vote would it not?
This is how this government thinks. It does not think. It is going to bring this bill forward. It is going to bring forward a bill on sentencing tomorrow. Tell the hon. member for Ottawa Centre about that. Again it is at second reading. It will go to committee and again come back to the House. It is going to bring a bill on the proceeds of crime with the same procedure. The minister announced a few minutes ago a bill on child pornography.
There is nothing wrong with these bills. They all have good parts in them. However, I am asking the hon.
member if he thinks the government is serious. I do not know how he feels about this, but if they should take one of these bills like the stalking bill or maybe one or two of the bills and concentrated on them and tried to get them through the House and through Parliament before Parliament ends then it could say to Canadians that it had actually done something.
I think it is going to go to an election campaign and say: "We have all these bills. We have a law and order agenda." It is fooling the Canadian people as it never really intended to pass the bills at all.
The short answer to that is if there is a will there is a way.

Madam Speaker, time is short and I just have a quick comment and then a question for the hon. member.
As a member of Parliament I am delighted to see this bill being brought in as legislation. There is some concern that I have with my colleagues on section 42 which prohibits intimidation that one will generally find is using violence or threats of violence against somebody or their spouse or children et cetera or watching somebody. I would like to see that strengthened and made more flexible in some regard so that it would be basically easier to prove. Intent is something I think we are really all concerned about.
The other aspect that I would like my hon. friend to comment on is that it is all very well to introduce legislation no matter how good it is, but there is concern about how quickly we can get things done even with legislation. I would ask my hon. colleague for Ottawa Centre if he really has thought about trying to get the federal government to work with the provinces so that, for example, items such as the issuing of a peace bond can be done much easier, more quickly and effectively.

I want to thank my colleague from Bonavis-ta-Trinity-Conception for his question. However, I see that you are standing up, Madam Speaker, to declare it one o'clock. Will we come back and answer the question afterwards?
May 6, 1993
