Mr. Speaker, the number one issue in Canada today is the deficit. That is why my private member's Bill C-301 is now at committee stage. It is one of only 5 per cent that ever make it that far.
The bill has three principles: government accountability for its spending; fair and efficient use of taxpayer dollars; and proper controls in place to eliminate cost overruns. They will help the Auditor General and every member of Parliament do the job they were hired and elected to do.
By ensuring a strict monitoring of funds spent by Parliament we will uncover wasteful spending and eliminate it. It is time for action.
The Conservatives are always complaining the Liberals have no ideas to control the deficit. I urge the finance minister to take a look at Bill C-301, supported by the Liberals, the NDP and Tory backbenchers. It is a modest and moderate proposal that is a step in the right direction. It is some common sense, for a change.

subtopic: INCOME TAX ON CHILD SUPPORT PAYMENTS
INCOME TAX ON CHILD SUPPORT PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, how would you like to pay income tax on income that is not
your own? If, like 500,000 individuals in Quebec, you receive child support payments, you have to add the total amount to your own income and pay tax on money that is not intended for your own use.
In fact, nothing is more unfair that this ostensibly equitable tax rule. The person paying child support, however, may deduct that amount from his income. In this case there is a tax advantage to being separated as opposed to being together as a family.
However, the person who receives the amount that is intended exclusively for the children, an amount set by the court according to the children's needs, is obliged to add this amount to her taxable income. Children are the real losers, because in a two-parent family, they would have the benefit of the equivalent of the total amount.
The Regroupement des femmes de l'Abitbi-Temisca-mingue feels it is clear that, as implemented, the rule fails to measure up to its original intent, and that for this reason, the government must find a solution that is satisfactory to all concerned.

Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley
Valley): Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to congratulate the people of Mackenzie, B.C. and other northern and remote communities in Saskatchewan and Manitoba on their campaign to see that the northern tax benefit is returned.
In Mackenzie a task force has been formed to lobby the government to have the phase-out of this program reversed and for a full return of the benefits.
It is regrettable that the Conservative government, supported by the Reform Party, is calling for the abolition of this benefit which is part of a tax fairness program, helps offset high living costs in recruiting professionals to isolated communities and has provided for some balance in the provision of government services which are often lacking in northern communities.
Petitions are being signed by hundreds of people and they are getting ready to make this an election issue. Keep up the fight for fairness, Mackenzie.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from a letter written by a soldier currently serving in Somalia. He said:
The general feeling over here is one of betrayal. I have seen more devastation, disease, corruption and disregard for human life than I ever thought possible! But that has changed, the Canadian soldiers serving here have given the next generation of Somalis hope, a safe place to live, the essentials to sustain life and a start in rebuilding their war-torn homeland.
We feel that we have become pawns to be played by some politicians to discredit others and further their own position. Soldiers here fear that if they must use force to protect themselves or the people we have been sent here to defend, that they will become another chess piece on the floor of the House of Commons, or be crucified by our own media, whom it appears would be happy to see young Canadian soldiers come home in body bags to get the better ratings!
To our soldiers, their wives, family and friends, I am proud of our peacekeepers. The actions of a few individuals, still to be determined, must not be allowed to overshadow the pride we have in our soldiers and their efforts and achievements.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for nine long years this government has been chopping away at programs and transfer payments that have increased the cost of a post-secondary education. At the same time it has consistently reduced annual funding for student summer employment programs.
Now Canada's students are forced to pay sharply increased tuition fees while the number of summer job opportunities continues to dwindle.
While the leadership candidates are delivering fancy slogans like "We Must Invest in our Young People" and "The Future is Everything" this Tory government sits here content in undermining the ability of our young people to forge ahead.
Canada is a proud democratic nation. This government's record on education has been nothing short of abysmal. It is time for change: change that will restore hope for Canada's young people in their educational system; change that will bring Canada back to the
forefront in educational standards; and change that will once again give Canada's young people a chance for higher learning and a chance to create jobs and build the industry of tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, it has been 30 years since the humble beginning of the Rusalka Dance Ensemble in Winnipeg.
Ukrainian dance is a very demanding art form. The intense concentration and precision as well as the expressiveness of the performers transport the viewers far beyond the boundaries of who they are to the ranges of where they might dream to be.
The Rusalka Dance Ensemble has over the past 30 years come to represent the overwhelming contributions made by Ukrainian settlers to the great nation of Canada. They came to Canada and became part of Canada, enriching this nation with great strength and commitment.
Ukrainian dance has travelled a long way from the steppes of the Ukraine to the prairies of Canada. Rusalka Dance Ensemble has fostered its links with the past and its enthusiasm for the future through gala concerts and performances that are as spectacular as they are exciting.
The Rusalka Dance Ensemble has become a preeminent ambassador for Canada throughout the world. Recognition of its achievements in its 30th year is well deserved.

Mr. Speaker, every year since 1990 the Minister of Finance has given us budget forecasts for 1992-93. In his 1990 budget he predicted a deficit of $21 billion for 1993; in 1991, he predicted a deficit of $24 billion and in 1992 his forecast was up to $27.5 billion. Now it is up to $35.5 billion.
On the evidence, we can say that the weatherman is better at making forecasts than the Minister of Finance.
I do not see why we should trust the minister's latest predictions. The evidence is there: federalism is not
May 6, 1993

worth it. It is getting Quebec into debt to the tune of seven or eight billion dollars annually.
That is why we want sovereignty for Quebec, and we want it as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw attention to a problem faced by snap bean growers in the Fraser Valley.
Over the last few years growers have experienced increasing losses due to white and grey mould infestations. These losses account for 25 per cent of the snap bean crop, with direct losses of $250,000 to the growers and over $1 million to the processors.
Growers in the U.S. can use the pesticide Ronalin D.F., which controls this type of infestation, while Canadian growers cannot. As a result Canadian growers cannot compete and will be out of business, losing $1 million to $2 million as well as taking 1,400 to 1,700 acres out of production.
Canadian processors will stop processing beans or process them in the U.S., using beans treated with the same chemical banned in Canada. This would result in an annual loss of $4 million to $7 million to British Columbia processors.
I would urgently request that the Departments of Agriculture and National Health and Welfare get together and resolve this problem as soon as possible. Planting and care for crops is governed by nature and hard work, not by a bureaucracy.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this do-nothing government lives up to its name when it comes to the disastrous state of the Canadian airline industry. Our airlines are engaged in destructive rather than healthy competition and both national carriers are generating huge losses.
The government's neglect of the airline industry has guaranteed that Canadians will pay the price for the lack
of service in this key transportation sector. Sudbury and other northern Ontario communities have already experienced the fall-out from airline deregulation: the cancellation of jet service, an increase in the use of small turbo prop aircraft, and the horrendous increase in air fares, the result of which has taken air travel out of the reach of ordinary Canadians.
Liberals believe that a Canadian airline industry should be competitive, Canadian controlled and provide safe and accessible air transportation services. A Liberal government would take corrective measures if any of these conditions did not exist.
Reliable air service is crucial for the economic development of all regions, including northern Ontario. I urge this government to take action now.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our troops assigned to peacekeeping activities in the former Yugoslavia risk their lives each day. They deserve our support and the support of all Canadians.
The Prime Minister is in Europe today to consult with the heads of state of countries allied with Canada on the explosive situation in Bosnia-Hercegovina.
The Prime Minister's consultations with our European allies are aimed at maximizing the safety of our troops, so that they can carry out their tasks under the mandate we received from the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker, at the legislative committee hearings on the North American free trade agreement yesterday the generic Canadian Drug Manufacturers' Association presented a legal opinion which demonstrated that NAFTA does not require that our generic drug legislation be repealed. This is the exact opposite of what the Minister for International Tirade has said from day one in defending Bill C-91.

May 6, 1993
If NAFTA does not require us to do away with generic drugs, then why has the Conservative government done it? The answer is that the U.S. government and the multinational drug companies consistently pressed until they found a Canadian government that would eliminate economical generic drugs in Canada and protect monopoly drug profits.
What about the next government? Canadians will want to know which of the opposition parties will guarantee the restoration of generic drugs. New Democrats make this commitment.
We have not heard from the Liberal Party, but its consumer affairs critic was reported in The Vancouver Sun of December 4 as saying that a Liberal government would not likely repeal Bill C-91.
Canadians already wonder if the Liberals really oppose medicare user fees. Do the Liberals really favour generic drugs? Stay tuned, and now over to you Jean.

Mr. Speaker, this country has two official languages. We have had an Official Languages Act for 25 years, as well as a Commissioner of Official Languages who acts as an ombudsman and monitors compliance with the act.
Today in 1993 there are still service agencies, national transportation agencies such as VIA Rail and Air Canada, that refuse to recognize the well-founded right of every Canadian to be served by these institutions in his own language, in other words, in English or in French.
When the commissioner of official languages tells us he has to take VIA Rail to court for its refusal to comply with the legislation, all Canadians should complain about this fact. Air Canada, which refuses to make its security announcements in both official languages, is also at fault. It is time this was stopped.
I would like to hear from the Tory leadership candidates, the former chairmen of the official languages committee, the member for Edmonton Southwest and the member for Halton-Peel, chairman of the official languages committee, what they intend to do to ensure
compliance with the Official Languages Act across this country.

Mr. Speaker, this week Canadians are celebrating National Forest Week. All across our country people are reflecting on the importance of our forests to our livelihood, our environment and our planet.
The theme, Our Common Ground, well illustrates the spirit of partnership so essential to our forest community. The concept of partnership was also reflected in the agreement that was recently signed by the federal Department of Forestry and the partners in New Brunswick of the Fundy model forest.
It includes industry, wood producers, local schools, municipal authorities and conservation groups. They will be working closely together to implement a sustainable management plan for a unique 400,000 hectare area in our province.
New Brunswick ranks second only to British Columbia in terms of the importance of forestry to the province's economy. I would like to pay tribute to the skill and dedication of the 13,000 people who work directly in our province's forest sector and I would like to thank them for their contribution to our prosperity and our future.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the conflict of interest bill is dead.
Earlier this week, the chairman of the special joint committee on conflict of interest wrote to members of the committee of both Houses informing us that the proposed conflict of interest act was no more.
The bill does not function as it is and the government House leader, on behalf of the government, refused to make the changes to make it work.
Canadians will have to ask themselves, why are Conservatives against having a conflict of interest act? Five times the Conservatives have introduced a conflict of interest bill. For the fifth time this bill will die. No
May 6, 1993

matter which Tory is in power, a Tory is a Tory is a Tory and they are not concerned with ethics. The proof is in the pudding.

Mr. Speaker, this morning I introduced a private member's bill to amend the Criminal Code.
This bill will make breach of any condition of parole or statutory release a criminal offence. Currently if someone breaches a condition of their parole that does not amount to a criminal offence. The Parole Board must be notified for a warrant to be issued for the arrest of that person.
With the amendment I am proposing, a police officer could act immediately to arrest an individual who is breaching any parole condition. This amendment will speed up police response times, especially when combined with the changes we are anticipating to the police computer system this summer.
These changes will give officers fast access to parole conditions. Quick response time is vital to community safety. Had this amendment already been in place, Kittye Schmidt and Ezio Faraone might still be alive. Both were victims of parolees who had breached parole conditions or were still on the loose. This bill will ensure that parole conditions actually mean something. I urge all members of the House to support this bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to mention a dynamic company in the composting industry.
Biomax Inc. offers composting processes based on performance monitoring according to well-defined criteria.
Besides offering a quality product, this organic-waste management company promotes and sells its own products and services, which accounts for its rapid growth in recent years.
Oral Questions
Hence Biomax's main focus on research. American composting practices were found to be less and less appropriate in Quebec because of our climate.
I salute the initiative of a company from our area which is focusing on protecting and enhancing our environment.

["Mr. Speaker, I can fully appreciate the member's concern for the safety of mariners. I can assure you that as we move along to examine the feasibility of privatizing the search and rescue operations that as usual in Transport Canada safety will be of the utmost importance. We will put in place the safeguards to ensure that we protect that safety."]

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
This morning United States President Clinton said the time for talk in Bosnia is over and he called for tougher measures through a unified collective action to stop the killing. The United Nations Security Council is meeting right now as we speak to consider brand new proposals. This raises serious questions for Canada, perhaps the most serious we have faced since the Korean war.
Is the government considering involvement in tougher military measures being proposed by the Americans? What does this mean for the security of our Canadians? We all need to have these answers and we need to have them now.
Will the Prime Minister immediately return to this country from his foreign tour and present to this House the government's position on these vital issues so that consent can be attained from Parliament on decisions that will have life and death consequences for our troops? We are tired of four-second clips from abroad. We need the answers here in Parliament.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, along with most other people in the world, I share the hon. member's concern about the turndown by the so-called Parliament of the Bosnian Serbs of the Vance-Owen peace plan and along with everybody else share concerns about what that might lead to.
I do not think it is helpful to use the kind of language the hon. member used. It is histrionics. He should appreciate the fact of how important the visit going on today between the Prime Minister and President Yeltsin is because Russia, as one of the members of the P-5, has a veto over Security Council actions and having an agreement or discussing the issues in Bosnia with Presi-

Oral Questions
dent Yeltsin is probably one of the most significant things the Prime Minister could be doing. That alone makes the trip an important and useful trip.
Canada, as we always have, will continue to look for an international solution and will continue to be helpful in terms of the discussions and negotiations going on in the UN and elsewhere. In terms of our troops, as the Prime Minister has said, the safety of Canadian troops is foremost in our minds.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the hon. minister that the most significant discussion the Prime Minister can have is with the Canadian people. They must be the ones who make decisions about the commitment of our troops.
If he has to talk to the Russian Prime Minister he can use a telephone. He can use the secret line, as the defence minister says she does all the time.

President Clinton says that tougher unified action is necessary. Our Canadian forces are exposed and, unfortunately, we are not getting complete information from the government.
I again ask the minister whether we support President Clinton's position. What is the situation of our forces?
I again ask the Prime Minister to return immediately to present Canada's position to Parliament before any decisions are made.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister said, we along with all of the countries that have troops in Yugoslavia are very concerned certainly about the circumstance of the troops and the peace and also concerned about any action taken of a military nature, what effect that would have on our troops and the desire to seek a permanent solution. Discussions are going on. Various alternatives are being suggested.
For the hon. member to suggest that all of those discussions be dropped, that conversations between the
Prime Minister and important world leaders like Yeltsin, Kohl, Mitterrand and Major in fact are trivial compared to coming in the House and listening a speech from the hon. member on this subject is absurd.
The Government of Canada will conduct itself properly. Our concern is for the troops. In this instance, as we always have in the past, we will work with the United Nations and other international partners to seek the best solution possible.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say to the hon. minister I have the utmost respect for this Parliament and the right of the Canadian people to have a voice and be heard through this Parliament.
Let me give an example of the kind of confusion that reigns in this government. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was reported this morning to have said that we will be offering more troops to go to Bosnia, but the parliamentary secretary to the House leader says we should pull out of Bosnia. The minister of defence said yesterday we do not have enough troops to go to Bosnia but we will send our aeroplanes.
I ask the minister or the Deputy Prime Minister: which is it? Are we going to send more ground troops or are we going to pull out? Are we going to participate in air strikes, as the defence minister seems to suggest? Is it not true and is it not the utmost common sense that at this crucial time affecting Canadians and our troops that the place of the Prime Minister is in Parliament and Parliament must have the right to decide before any decisions are taken to commit further troops or put our troops at further risk?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the tone, the language, the accusatory words used by the hon. member put a lie to any suggestion that reasonable debate and discussion could occur here, not as long as the hon. member uses that tactic in terms of this important subject.
Just to correct the record, what the Prime Minister said in respect of further troops was: "Obviously Canada has responded in the past and would carefully examine
May 6, 1993

any request for further assistance from the Secretary General." That is what the Prime Minister said.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member sits there, says he asked a serious question and yet he barracks from his seat and says please treat us seriously, we deserve it. The hon. member has to earn that seriousness and he does not do it by the behaviour he is exemplifying here.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: That is disrespectful of democracy.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: You've got to earn it.
I said your minister of external affairs.

speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Use an opposition day.

Mr. Speaker, the peace operation in Bosnia is at a very critical point. Concern is continuing to rise in the country regarding our participation because there are many warning signals and no debate. The latest of these is an expression of concern for the safety of our troops by the Canadian forces commander in Bosnia.
My question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. What is the mandate of our troops in Bosnia and what is the government plan for our 2,400 troops there in the event of a western air strike?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is postulating that a western air strike is something imminent and will occur. No such thing.
Discussions are going on in terms of that option and other options in view of the very, very unfortunate result in the so-called Bosnian Serbian Parliament.
Reality is that what we all want is a cessation of the hostilities, the stopping of this vicious ethnic cleansing and the atrocities that are occurring. Canada is there under the UN auspices doing our best in terms of providing humanitarian aid to the refugees and to try and effect the cease-fire in places like Srebrenica and so on.
Oral Questions
We continue to engage in discussions with our allies. That is what the Prime Minister is doing, that is what the Secretary of State for External Affairs is doing, that is what the Department of External Affairs is doing and our ambassadorial staff in the various capitals.
Hopefully from this and discussions a plan will arise that is workable. Hopefully the Bosnian Serbs will come to realize their current posture is simply unsustainable and will lead to horrendous damage to themselves as well as to others and we will find a solution.
In the meantime, Canada's first priority is to make sure our troops are not put at undue risk and that they are well equipped for that. As events develop in the hours and days and weeks ahead we will respond accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, we have to be the only country in the world that would have put our troops in the line of fire in a foreign country without as much as a word of debate in Parliament.
With the three key ministers, the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence, removed from the show, I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister: Who in Canada is in political charge of this sensitive operation at this critical time? Who has the total picture? Will the Deputy Prime Minister initiate an immediate debate in Parliament on one of the most important issues in the history of this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week there was an opposition day on this subject. I think it was exactly a week ago today. The lead speaker for the Liberal Party gave a loud, boisterous and accusatory speech and then left the Chamber never to come back.
If the hon. member is suggesting that that kind of thing is helpful to our troops and if we believed that kind of thing would be helpful to peace in Yugoslavia and to the security of our forces there, we would certainly engage in it immediately.
In the meantime, as the Prime Minister has said, we are not fundamentally opposed to a rational, sane, objective discussion of the issues there, but in fact there has never been any evidence from the other side that

May 6, 1993
Oral Questions
they are interested in anything else but trying to tarnish the reputation of this government.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, what would be helpful not only to this House but to Canadians would be to have a Minister of National Defence who is prepared to stand up and be accountable in this Parliament instead of campaigning across the country for the leadership.
She was in committee yesterday.
I think we might remind ourselves that we have a long-standing rule that we do not refer to the absence of any particular member in the House. I would just ask both sides of the House to respect it.

Mr. Speaker, I was merely taking my direction from the government House leader on this one.
Yesterday, in the wake of the tragic decision of the Bosnian Serb Parliament to reject the Vance-Owen peace plan, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said: "Our focus will be very sharp on new and stronger measures." We know that those measures may include air strikes and the lifting of the embargo on the Muslims in Bosnia.
Given the profound significance of either of these steps for the safety of Canadian troops, precisely what is the response of Canada to these developments, and specifically what are the contingency plans that the minister referred to yesterday in the House in the event that the peace plan has broken down?
It has broken down at this point, and Canadians are entitled to know what our response is to protect the safety of Canadian forces?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with regard to the hon. member's preamble we do not take attendance around here, but I think the Minister of National Defence has been here more often than he has.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In terms of the options available-
I wonder if on both sides of the House we could just leave that aspect of the debate to some other place and get on with the questions and the answers. We know what the rule is.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
As the Minister of National Defence, myself, the Prime Minister and others have said on many occasions, the Canadian forces in Yugoslavia have contingency plans in place that will permit them to protect themselves in the event hostilities take an unfortunate turn.
With regard to proposals being put forward by the Secretary of State of the United States, those proposals and others are under active discussion at the UN between the Prime Minister and President Yeltsin, between other leaders of the western world and indeed leaders all over the world.
The final position that might be taken by the UN is not known. It is not known to the UN itself. Canada is making sure that its views are being heard at the important places where they should be heard. When in fact a decision has been taken one can anticipate that Canada, as it always has in the past, will act in concert with the rest of the world through the United Nations. Hopefully those plans will lead to the kind of lasting peace and at least in the short term the cessation of hostilities in Yugoslavia which we are all after.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. minister says Canada's views are being made known in the appropriate place. Surely the families of Canadian troops in Bosnia, Canadian troops themselves, and most importantly Canadians, have a right to answers to those questions in Parliament and not behind closed doors somewhere. We still do not know what the position of the Canadian government is on these issues.
Yesterday the Bosnian Serb information minister said that the Americans were only bluffing about military action and they would never intervene. Given that there is a crisis under way now, that there is no water in Srebrenica, that the towns of Zepa and Goradze are under siege even as we speak, I want to ask this government if we are prepared to show some leadership and at the very least call within the United Nations for the establishment of safe havens and humanitarian corridors to prevent the kind of ethnic cleansing which has been taking place in Bosnia. Will we finally put some
May 6, 1993

teeth into our call for bringing these war criminals to justice?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been calling for actions along those lines for months and months and months. That is what the Canadian troops are there for; that is what they are trying to do in Srebrenica.
I agree with the hon. member. It is most disturbing that the so-called Bosnian Serb Parliament has taken that position. I believe they are wrong, hopefully not but perhaps tragically wrong, in their assertion that the rest of the world lacks the will to take the necessary action to stop the atrocities from going on there. That is a very dangerous position for them to take.
In the meantime I think the hon. member would realize that the most prudent position for the Government of Canada is to continue to discuss with our allies various alternatives. If Canada as the hon. member suggests should come out with its position, every other country would have the same right. How would that aid in bringing about the kind of resolution to this problem we all want to see?

My final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, is for the same minister.
Certainly we agree that Canadians have a right to be consulted. In light of that I want to ask this minister- and I will not comment on the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs-
Oh, oh.

The House knows perfectly well why we have a rule that we do not make comments about members who may not be in their seats at any given time. The reason for it is that members and ministers have many things to do and cannot always be here.
I have asked both sides of the House to respect that. We are not advancing what is essentially a very serious series of questions and answers by constantly making reference and breaking a rule that we all know is there.
Oral Questions
I hope the hon. member will take that into account and put his question.

Mr. Speaker, the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade is surely entitled to basic facts about what is happening in Bosnia.
This morning the standing committee unanimously voted to report to the House that the Department of External Affairs was in contempt of Parliament if it did not make briefings available to members of that standing committee.
What does the government have to hide? Why is it not prepared to ensure that members of Parliament on the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade are given the basic facts about the role and the safety of Canadian troops in Bosnia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is nothing to hide and there is no reason to raise undue concerns about the safety of our troops in Bosnia.
We can be sure that the professionals in the Department of National Defence-Canada has more experience in this kind of thing than any other country in the world-have the plans in place to ensure that our troops are not put at undue risk.
In terms of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade, the minister is in Croatia today. She has been in Bosnia. She will be going on to Somalia and coming back to Canada. As indicated she will be prepared to appear before the committee next week and to answer any and all questions the hon. member and other members might have.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's tabling of the Department of National Defence report on sexual harassment confirmed that 26.2 per cent of women in the forces had experienced some sort of sexual harassment. Also it confirmed that too few of those harassed were using the complaint procedure.
My question is for the Deputy Prime Minister. Could he tell us what in this new report will encourage these people to come forward and actually use the complaint procedures?

May 6, 1993
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Department of National Defence has recommended as a result of the report three significant changes.
There will be an appointment of an harassment adviser. There will be a change to the Queen's regulations to allow for an adviser to assist the complainant both during the complaint and the investigation stages. There will be a reporting system. A tracking system will be implemented to monitor and record the number of complaints made by members of the forces.
They will be implementing a program of education and training to raise the awareness and really teach some people exactly what harassment is and why it is of such serious concern.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. House leader for his answer. I would be happier if it were not for the fact that these kinds of recommendations mirror quite closely the Treasury Board guidelines that have been in place with this government for some time.
The problem is the Treasury Board guidelines similar to these are not being enforced. Transgressors in the Public Service of Canada are not being disciplined.
My question therefore is for the Acting Prime Minister. Again what measures will he take to ensure that all those who report cases of harassment will be taken seriously and that those very guidelines and rules he is talking about are going to be enforced? We have no reason to think so thus far.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the report was just released yesterday and the Department of National Defence only had it a day or two before that I guess these are the changes it has put in place.
It is a bit unfair, having put in these changes in terms of National Defence and having indicated they would take the problem seriously, for the hon. member to conclude it is all a charade and that National Defence does not intend to have these measures work.
I do not think the hon. member has any evidence to justify that in terms of the Department of National Defence. She should wait and see and be objective in her assessment.

Mr. Speaker, currently there are 1.2 million Canadians living in inadequate shelter. CMHC's own corporate plan has concluded that economic hardships will cause a growing number of Canadians to live in inadequate housing. With continual lay-offs across the country these problems are felt in an increasing way by major urban centres in Canada: Vancouver, Winnipeg, Montreal, Toronto and Halifax.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance why this government is abandoning its federal-provincial obligation to provide equal access to affordable housing across Canada.

Why is this government abandoning the poor who need social housing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government is not abandoning the poor.
We are supporting 650,000 units of social housing at an annual cost of some $2 billion. Under the 35-year subsidy program that has been in existence it creates a tremendous cost exposure on the future taxpayers of Canada.
For example, for the $41 million that will be invested in social housing this year, when that is paid out over a 35-year period it will impose a $1.3 billion burden on the future taxpayers of Canada.
What we have outlined in the budget are new approaches and new ways and means to deal with the social housing issue which can be done on a more affordable basis.

Mr. Speaker, the minister might say what he wants but the facts speak for themselves.
May 6, 1993

Last year he killed co-op housing. This year he killed new funding for any social housing altogether. This effectively shelves the cost sharing federal-provincial programs that include housing for seniors and the disabled, RRAP and the emergency repair program.
How can the government justify cancelling these programs without first instituting cost efficient housing alternatives? There are many, and we have proposed many such as public private partnerships.
When will the government bring all the stakeholders to the table for a national housing policy and a national housing program so we can all work together to house Canadians?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would hope this would be one of the subjects that could be discussed at the federal-provincial level when finance ministers meet to deal with the challenges of the deficit and the debt, the burden that imposes upon all Canadians, and to organize in a co-operative way practical solutions to deal with the problem.
This is an area that is clearly of joint responsibility. I have to remind the hon. member in terms of providing housing with respect to the aboriginal people on reserves, the disabled and those responsible for violence against women, that those provisions will still be provided under the social housing program.
We all have to recognize that while we are very supportive and indeed want to enhance all our social programs, we have a very serious debt and deficit problem which we have to handle and manage. I hope my hon. friend understands that. We are going to try to do the best we can in managing the resources that are available and trying to get more value and benefit from those scarce resources.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have just received the decision from the United States on the softwood lumber tariff dispute.
It seems this dispute goes on and on. The ruling today sends the decision back to the commerce department to
Oral Questions
report back again in 90 days and to continue the harassment of Canadian softwood lumber exports to the United States.
What specific steps are the minister and the government going to take to ensure that Canadian softwood lumber exports to the United States will not continually be harassed as this decision does? It just puts off resolving this matter for another 90 days.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Thade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really quite surprised at the tone of my hon. friend's question.
What we have in the decision from the softwood panel is one that is very positive for Canada. Yes, there is a remand, a referral back to the International Trade Commission in the United States on a number of issues, practically all the issues.
However, I would say to my hon. friend the arguments put forward by Canada and other Canadian interveners were largely accepted by the panel, and this is a positive thing. I should call something to my friend's attention since he chooses to ignore it.
We would not have had the opportunity of putting these arguments if we had not had the free trade agreement. It is because of the free trade agreement that we had this opportunity to put our case forward and get a positive response for Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary for the minister is this.
Given that the U.S. lumber coalition and other authorities in the United Stated have already indicated they intend to launch an extraordinary challenge of this decision, to keep the fight going for the United States, can the minister tell the House if he has assurances from the new administration in Washington that President Clinton will drop this tariff dispute now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason I was somewhat late coming into the House for Question Period was that I had just received the decision. I have not had a chance to discuss it in any way with members of the United States administration.

May 6, 1993
Oral Questions
I can tell my hon. friend that I had raised the matter with the administration prior to the decision. I pointed out to them that in the face of this constraint on exports of Canadian softwood lumber to the United States, the price of lumber had gone up. It has almost doubled in the last year and a half. There has been no new production of any substance in the United States. In fact, some of the environmental concerns that are held in the United States are constraining production there.
I have pointed out very strongly that it is in the interests of the United States' economy to drop this and I would encourage them to do so.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister for International Trade.
Last Friday another Ontario manufacturing plant announced its closure. The most productive Mack truck plant in North America is closing its doors and two ministers in this House said it had absolutely nothing to do with the free trade agreement.
I have in my hand a copy of the free trade agreement. In the free trade agreement, item 8701.20.00, the Conservative government abolished the duty of 9.2 per cent on road tractors for semi-trailers, allowing Mack truck to bring their trailers into Canada duty free.
How can the ministers continue to claim in the House that these jobs are not being lost as a result of free trade when their own free trade agreement has given an open door policy to Mack truck to come into Canada with no duties?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not happy when I see a factory like Mack truck or others scaling back or shutting down their operations.
I think my hon. friend should take a broader view, if that is possible, and look at some of the successes we have had under the free trade agreement. Last year for example, our exports were up 13.6 per cent in a year of a slow economy. Just to give my friend some broader numbers, Alberta's exports to the United States since
the free trade agreement came in are up 52 per cent; Saskatchewan's are up 44 per cent; Ontario up-
She's from Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: If my hon. friend would listen, I would tell him what has happened in Ontario. Exports are up 29 per cent.
Tell us about Mack trucks.

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: My hon. friend says when I give him the good news he says he wants to talk about something else. Let us look at-
The hon. member, supplementary.

Mr. Speaker, I want to direct my supplementary to the Minister of State for Finance and Privatization who is spreading other misinformation around the House about the availability of jobs in Oakville at the Ford plant.
Because of the re-tooling.

The minister responsible for revenue who is allowing these trucks to go through duty free stated last week to those who lost jobs at Mack truck: "You lose some, you win some. They are hiring now at Ford as a result of a $1 billion investment. They are hiring right now. Why don't you tell the Mack truck workers to go and look for jobs at Ford?"
Minutes ago I spoke to the labour management at Ford. Not only is it not hiring but it has 500 people at Ford on lay-off.
Why is the minister of revenue spreading misinformation and telling Mack truck workers, who have just had the door slammed in their face, that they can go down the street to Ford when Ford is also on lay-off? Why are you giving up on the workers of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one is giving up on the workers of Canada. The free trade agreement is helping the workers of Canada.
Let me give my hon. friend one specific example. Does she not accept the fact that the reason there have been problems with Ford right now is because the plant is in transition in retooling for the billion dollar investment that Ford has made in Oakville. There is another billion dollar investment by Ford in Windsor.
May 6, 1993

Right across the street, Lear seating has opened a new plant completely, creating 650 direct and indirect new jobs simply to supply that Ford investment. This is an example of where the investment by Ford has created the opportunity for investments by others. With Lear seating, 650 is quite a bit larger than what has resulted from the lay-offs at Mack.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance who must know that the unemployment rate among Canadian youth jumped to nearly 18 per cent last month. Another 28,000 young Canadians are out there loafing around as a result of this government's brutal policies.
In Newfoundland alone, youth unemployment skyrocketed last month from 31 per cent to 38 per cent.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance why there was not something in last week's budget to deal with this job crisis and to get those young people working?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think young Canadians as well as all Canadians are deeply concerned about the debt and the deficit problem. At least when I travel across the country it is a matter they are increasingly concerned about because ultimately the responsibility will rest on their shoulders.
We have to be realistic in reducing government expenditures while at the same time bolstering economic growth, creating new jobs and new economic activity, and taking advantage of the opportunities that occur as a result of the newly emerging economy.
The hon. member is very clearly aware that in the December statement we took initiatives to stimulate the small business sector, to invest in more training and skills upgrading programs, and to invest in infrastructure.
Through the very hard work and the untiring efforts of the minister of fisheries, he has been very instrumental in helping meet the very serious crises in the fishing industry in Newfoundland and in other Atlantic-

I think we must move on. The hon. member, a supplemental.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I say to the minister that those young people are also concerned about their education and about careers. That is where his policies are failing those people, failing an entire generation absolutely and shamelessly.
Since 1985, for example, funding for the Challenge program, the SEED program, has been axed by more than 50 per cent. Student jobs have been wiped out right, left and centre by this minister. Education opportunities have disappeared because the government has been tampering with the student loan policy and the transfer payments to provinces.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance, why does the government not stop this vicious attack on young people and start giving them a break on their education and on their search for jobs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Pauline Browes (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond concerning the Challenge '93 program. The fact of the matter is that there has been an increase of $5.1 million in the funding for youth employment in Challenge '93 for this year. As well, over 400 youth employment centres have been established. We are very pleased that so many employers are assisting in helping youth.
Besides the government assisting youth employment, a number of private sector, public sector and non-profit groups are helping with the Challenge '93 to a total of some 57,000 jobs for young people this summer. We are very pleased with that and I would expect that the member might compliment the government on this increased funding for youth.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of trade.
Yesterday in the legislative committee on NAFTA the assistant deputy attorney general told the committee that GATT tariff item 2201, which is ordinary natural waters of all kinds other than sea water, is included in the NAFTA agreement as a commodity of trade. He also acknowledged there is no exclusive provision in the agreement to exempt the large scale export of water as a commodity of trade.

May 6, 1993
Oral Questions
I would like to ask the Minister for International Trade this. He managed to get specific exemptions for the export of raw logs. He managed to get specific exemptions for the export of unprocessed fish. Why has he failed to get specific exemptions for the bulk export of Canadian waters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this one keeps going on and on. The New Democratic Party does not accept it is a simple fact of Canadian government policy that we will not allow any exports in bulk of water.
In addition to that, it is a specific part of the legislation for both the free trade agreement and the NAFTA that there will be no exports of large bodies of water.
My hon. friends in the New Democratic Party, in face of the fact that there is no desire on the part of the Americans to seek exports of water, are saying that we should negotiate something that is contrary to our legislation, contrary to our policy.
I ask them what they would put on the table to gain that? Would they put on culture, would they put on the investment restrictions, would they put on the supply management systems?

Last year the cost of crime to our society was in excess of $12 billion to $14 billion. That is a great sum of money that is wasted. When we look at the causes of violence and crime in our society, it always brings us back to the same question. It is the question of education. Many of

Mr. Speaker, I rise as justice critic for the federal New Democratic Party to speak on Bill C-126.
We have already heard an eloquent speech this morning from my colleague, the member for New Westminster-Burnaby. I am going to make some references to some of the things she said in her speech.
Let me say right away that we in the New Democratic Party will support this bill. We would like to see the bill passed before Parliament dissolves for the next election. We regret that the government did not bring this bill forward sooner.
This bill in many ways is in response to the private member's bill and the pressure that has been brought by
the member for New Westminster-Burnaby, various people in the women's movement in Canada and other people who want to see this bill passed.
We want to see the bill passed too. We are going to press that it go to committee this afternoon, we get some hearings in committee but we get it back in the House and try to pass it before Parliament breaks.
The bill deals with two real aspects. The first aspect is family violence and violence against women. The bill makes stalking a new crime of criminal harassment. It will be punishable by up to five years in prison.
In the second part of the bill, if a woman flees an abusive partner and takes her children with her she cannot be found guilty of child abduction even if the children are not in direct danger.
The third part of the first section of the bill says that before a man charged with assaulting his partner can be released on bail the judge will have to consider imposing a condition that he not return to the family home or other place or communicate with the victim or other witnesses.
We heard the member for New Westminister-Burnaby today give detail upon detail of instances where women have been harassed and indeed terrorized. As I said this morning, I started my career as a Crown attorney in Vancouver and I recall the difficulties we had with the law with respect to threats and some of the attitudes there such as: "These women are just complaining. They will not charge these fellows anyway. You will never convict them," and so on.
The fact is that in murder cases, especially for women, the murderer is likely to be the partner or ex-partner of the woman. There was a terrifying case in my own riding in Coquitlam, which is a suburb of Vancouver. A woman called Alexandra Pesic worked in a medical office. She was allegedly being harassed by her ex-husband, but she definitely was being harassed. She complained and nothing happened. Then she was brutally killed right on Cottonwood Avenue in Coquitlam. The whole community realized that an instance of harassment and terrorizing had ended in the worst possible circumstances.
Most women, thank God, are not killed in these circumstances, but many women are harassed and terrorized. When love turns to hate it often has strange consequences.
May 6, 1993

As I said, we regret that this bill was not brought forward sooner. I will just quote from a recent editorial in The Victoria Times-Colonist. It reads:
The timing is terrible, the political sincerity is suspect, the drafting
is sloppy and the efficacy dubious.
If Blais was so anxious to see this bill become law, why did he delay
its introduction so long? He first mentioned it in early February.
There was a similar article in The Edmonton Sun which questions the purposes of the government. It reads:
A cynic might say this is pure political bluster.
The thought is out there that while the government is bringing this in at the last moment it is not really serious. We want to make the government serious. All parties in the House want to make the government serious and we want to see this bill passed.
There are other parts to the bill as well. The bill also deals with child abuse. I would have liked to have seen the bill split. The first part deals with family violence. We could get on with that and do it now and the stalking bill. We could then come back and do a better job, in my view, than the bill does with the child abuse aspects because it is long overdue that we deal with this. As a matter of fact the justice committee right now as I speak is doing a review of sexual assault and of course some of it is in this bill. That is not a very good way to proceed is it?
Let me talk a little bit about what the bill proposes to do. On child abuse, people convicted of sex crimes against children could face up to a lifetime ban from going near day care centres, school yards, playgrounds, parks or bathing areas where children are likely to be found. They would also be prohibited from seeking or obtaining employment that involves a position of trust or authority over children.
The bill also mentions that children who testify in cases of sexual abuse or violence would be allowed to have a support person such as a relative or friend close to them to ease the court experience. Some judges now permit this informally, but it in fact will be put directly into the law.
I have just put my hands on one of the transcripts from the justice committee hearing the other day. Monica Rainey who is with a group from British Columbia called Citizens Against Child Exploitation is one of the people who took 5,000 teddy bears to the steps of the Victoria
Government Orders
legislature as a protest about the 10 per cent of children in B.C. who are sex abuse victims. This is a serious matter. Society is now taking it seriously. Where children are sexually abused as young kids, often in the family or people associated with the family, they often go on to be perpetrators of sexual abuse.
Monica said this, and I think it is worth quoting and bringing before the House: "Would you be moved by the story of the little Alberta girl who was not allowed to testify on her own behalf? She was six years of age. This was just this past year. The judge wanted her to pronounce a word to signify that she was qualified to testify in court. She stuttered so badly she could not say the word he wanted her to say. Therefore she was denied the opportunity to speak on her own behalf." It goes on: "Her mother said that the reason she stuttered so badly is because her father performed oral sex on her since she was an infant." Thankfully in this case the Crown proceeded even though the man was acquitted. They have been granted a second trial where hopefully she will have the opportunity to speak. The law clarifies this.
There are terrible cases and terrible incidents. It is just amazing that these things are happening in this country and the law has to deal with them. This bill proposes to do that.
The bill also states that a judge would be allowed to prevent people who represent themselves, that is without a lawyer, from cross-examining the victims of child sexual abuse. The judge would be able to appoint counsel to do the questioning in order to be sensitive to the questioning of the particular people who after all are victims testifying at a trial. Judges would not have to warn jurors about the dangers of convicting a person based on the testimony of children that is not corroborated by their evidence. The child's evidence would be evaluated in the same way as that of the adults. These are interesting and important propositions that do need some detailed study.
We agree with the thrust of these propositions but I think they need some detailed study in committee. Now is not the time to do that when Parliament is dying and when we already have another part of the bill that we are dealing with and the justice committee is looking at the matter of child abuse right now. I would prefer that we
