law or some other aspects of law that is not dealing with the family."
I cite for the government's benefit from what is almost one of its own house organs: The Globe and Mail. This is an editorial in Toronto's national newspaper on April 28, 1993 that refers to the member for New Westminster- Burnaby:
Ms. Black's concerns are well founded. Re-read that definition of criminal harassment, and see how many examples of legitimate, desirable public protest it covers. If a group of environmentalists repeatedly visit a polluting factory, and they are, as protesters are wont to be, rude and angry, should they be charged with criminal harassment? If strikers in front of a business protest replacement workers, never resorting to violence but day after day crying "scab", is that criminal harassment? No. The legislation must make it clear that unpleasant but legitimate protests are not its target.
All that is required is for the bill to include an exemption or clarification, explaining that labour disputes and other forms of political speech and action, sometimes boisterous, passionate affairs, are not covered by this bill.
The Globe would not say "scabs" would it?
We propose to bring in such an amendment and I ask the government to consider it fairly. We even have the support of the national newspaper, The Globe and Mail. I do not know if that is a good argument for it or a bad one.
There are already two stalking provisions existing in the Criminal Code and they have different penalties. This has to be clarified because one of them, in section 423, is not repealed by the bill and has a summary conviction penalty only. So the judge may be confused. Does he or she apply that or does he or she apply the new stalking provision?
We talked this morning and the hon. member in her letter to the minister talked about the need to educate police forces and the judiciary about violence against women. This is very important. One can pass all the legislation one likes but that is only one part of it. One has to implement the legislation and have people understand the implementations: how does one implement it, how important the legislation is, what it entails and what Parliament is getting at.
We are seeing changes. We talked this morning about impaired driving. I mentioned when I was a young prosecutor when I kind of winked a little bit and said: "Well, it was just one of the boys having a few drinks." Now society takes impaired driving very seriously. The penalties have been increased. There is a mandatory jail
May 6, 1993

sentence. Kids say to their fathers or mothers: "Wait a minute. Do not get in that car if you have been drinking because it is dangerous." We have moved the society. Society has been educated there and starts to understand.
This has to happen with the issue of stalking and threatening women. There is too often a certain notion even among the judiciary, although that is changing. It is among the police, although that is changing too. There is still the notion out there that it just happens in a family dispute. It is just a family dispute or it is just going to happen and there is nothing much one can do about it.
The instances that the member for New Westminster-Burnaby revealed to the House today were simply astounding. It went all the way from leaving rats on the door to locking flowers in the car to consistent phone calls-300 phone calls a week-to terrorizing women to following them to following the car of an ex-wife because she got a visit from a friend and the thinking was that the friend was a new suitor. The member said this morning that it is based on a sense of this notion of always having power and control over women, of possession.
It is hard for me to understand this not being a woman. However, when I heard the women in the House talking eloquently about this I began to realize that it is really awful to be stalked and to be terrorized. They go to the police only to be told: "Oh, well, forget about it." They might say instead: "There is nothing we can do."
If we pass this bill there will be an effective, I hope, weapon in the hands of women so that they can fight back on this. That is why it is so important to pass this bill.
I believe I have summarized some of the problems with the bill. I suggested that it be split up. I suggested a number of amendments that could be brought in. I really feel a bit disheartened by the government in the past week or so. We have a bill on sentencing. We are going to do another bill on proceeds of crime. We are going to do a bill on child pornography. We are going to do a bill this afternoon on psychoactive drugs. They are all going to go to committee. I have the feeling that this is all just a ruse to make the government look good, to make it look as if it has a program. Yet none of it will see the light of day
Government Orders
because it was brought in too late and at the end of a Parliament that will not have enough time to consider it.
I say let us pick-this is good leadership and what the Minister of Justice should do-one or two of these bills and get them through Parliament. The opposition and we in the New Democratic Party will co-operate and we can bring these laws in, especially in this area where there is a bill whose time has come to protect women and other people from the terror and stalking they suffer from.
Having said that I will sit down and hopefully we can put this bill through in principle this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, this is a bill that, although I will certainly be supporting it, is not one that really impresses me or impresses the millions of victims and potential victims of violent criminals in this country.
There is no doubt that we need legislation against stalking. Vulnerable members of our society have surely been denied protection for too long from being hounded and intimidated by former spouses or just by neighbourhood degenerates.
The stalking issue has been addressed in considerable detail in this morning's and this afternoon's debate so I would like to focus my remarks on other issues of great concern to Canadians which are also contained in this bill.
Unfortunately other elements of this bill will be of little relief to parents who leave their children in child care or allow them to play in local parks and other facilities. This bill provides for up to a lifetime ban on convicted sex offenders to frequent day care centres, school grounds, play grounds, community centres, public parks or bathing areas where children are likely to be found or to seek and obtain employment that involves a position of trust or authority over children. The bill also provides for the court to impose no prohibition at all.
This is all very nice and is certainly a modest improvement on the current situation. However concerned parents will be quick to ask why a convicted sex offender who is considered sufficiently dangerous to be banned from being around children is allowed on the street at all.

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
Why is it that someone who has proven himself to be a predator of children should be given the freedom and opportunity to destroy more young lives? There is nowhere in our cities that children cannot easily be found by one of these sick individuals.
It is not sufficient to declare only a few areas as safe zones nor will these areas be any safer. How will these people be identified if they are free to travel throughout the country? How are police forces going to keep track of all these criminals as they maraud from district to district, especially as police resources are being cut back? More important, are child molesters really going to be thwarted in their search for new prey?
On the way to Ottawa there is a McDonald's restaurant with a play area for children. Can this law stop an offender from going to his local fast food restaurant, shopping mall or ice cream parlour?
I support this bill because it provides police forces with an additional, though insufficient, weapon against the degenerate filth that roams our streets.
I do not think that this bill will substantially reduce the number of child victims of repeat sex offenders. Bill C-126 will fail to provide children with the security they deserve because it fails to address the dilemma that has allowed so many rapists and child molesters onto the streets of our cities and towns.
Many of my constituents fervently believe that if the National Parole Board were in charge of the Metro Zoo, wild animals would be all over the streets of Toronto. They are in a state of perpetual disgust at not only the light sentences that sex offenders receive but the unconscionable level of early release.
Not long ago, the Minister of Justice told Canadians that untreated sex offenders have a 30 per cent likelihood of reoffending. What that means to Canada's women and children is that for every 100 rapists and child molesters who are released by the National Parole Board, at least 30 women and children will be raped or molested. The National Parole Board has to know that every time they release a batch of 100 predators that they are guaranteeing that 30 women or children will be victimized.
Canadians are often bewildered by these decisions and by a government that forces them to keep children within easy range of known sexual predators.
We all know the cause of the current level of victimization is really a financial one. It is horrendously expensive to keep sex offenders behind bars. That is why the government prefers the kind of legislation we are discussing today, which makes some effort to restrict the availability of prey for those offenders who are driven to hunt children. It is the cheap way out, to talk about protecting children while not having to spend the money for proper protection.
Federal authorities can open the cages of sex offenders without sufficient regard for the threat these predators pose to unsuspecting citizens. Responsibility for their actions is not borne by the government but instead by innocent women and children. Victims will see their assailants recaptured, convicted and then released after another insufficient stretch of imprisonment.
These releases will save the federal Treasury thousands and perhaps millions of dollars, but will also create countless victims. I believe governments cannot balance their books by allowing sex offenders to claim victim after victim with only short interruptions in prison. It is time the government placed its highest priority on the safety of children. The key to keeping children safe is the key to the cages of sex offenders.
No less daunting is the task of dealing with stalkers. Women are stalked not necessarily by released sex offenders but by people they have once trusted or admired. Here we tread on a behaviour that often ends in tragedy.
Representatives of some women's groups have questioned the potential for this bill to be turned against the very people it is clearly intended to help. They wonder if the woman repeatedly calling an ex-husband for overdue child support could be prosecuted under this act. This will always be a problem when a law specifically intended to protect women is phrased in gender neutral language. The tragedy this bill responds to is not the presence of harassing behaviour. The tragedy is the violence that too often comes at the end of an extended period of stalking. By restricting stalking we can hope to protect women from eventual violence.
Perhaps the bill would be improved if it were specific on who is likely to be a threat to whom and not be so given to political correctness. Since 1974 over 400 women were murdered by men who had been stalking them. That is the issue that needs to be addressed. We should
May 6, 1993

adopt amendments that make this more clear, less ambiguous and more direct.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in the debate on this very important initiative, Bill C-126.
It is an omnibus bill which would do a number of things. It would create a new offence of criminal harassment for stalking by prohibiting communicating with or following someone with the intent to harass them. It would also prohibit sex offenders from frequenting places where children congregate and from being employed in positions of trust over children. It would also facilitate the ability of child witnesses to give evidence in court.
I want to say right from the beginning that we support this legislation. As a matter of fact it follows very quickly on the tail of the legislation of my colleague, the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby, who some time ago introduced a private member's bill that was actually much tougher when it came to stalking.
However, after a lot of urging from individuals, victims, women's groups and organizations that have raised concerns about stalking for a long time, the government now is taking some action. I want to say we appreciate that.
However I must question the government's sincerity. After all, we are here at the end of a mandate and the stalking of women is not a new issue. We have heard some eloquent presentations during the day by people describing the horror associated with stalking and women being harassed and treated in a most barbaric fashion by ex-spouses or by ex-partners. I remember the example of the singer Anne Murray and an oddball from the prairies who stalked her for years and years. He was convicted 11 times, yet it continues because the laws of the country are inadequate.
We do not have to look very far to see what other jurisdictions have done. I believe 29 states in the United States have enacted their own anti-stalking legislation to protect women from being unfairly harassed by men and ex-partners and treated in the most disgusting way with phone calls in the middle of the night, hour after hour, people dropping off dead animals on their steps just to remind them that they are spying on them, following them on foot, driving behind their cars and tracking them
Government Orders
from place to place. We have even seen movies that reflect this horrible activity, and we have no laws to stop it.
There are some rather inadequate passages in the existing Criminal Code that make some vague effort to do this, but in essence the police are helpless. The laws simply are not there. A number of states in the United States have taken action on this and have legislation in process. Here we are on the eve of the end of a mandate and the government takes this initiative. I am somewhat suspect but I will say we are pleased that it is here now.
I want to say on behalf of the New Democratic Party we will do whatever we have to do. We will debate all night long. We will sit here over the weekend to ensure that this legislation passes so women can be protected from this hideous experience so many people have to put up with.
It is interesting that less than two weeks ago I had the opportunity to spend a good part of a day with various RCMP officers from the Kamloops detachment. We were talking about a number of issues. I asked them to what extent stalking took place in our region. They indicated they received calls on a regular basis and had been for many years. They felt quite helpless in their ability to respond satisfactorily. They pointed out, like everyone else, the inappropriate legislation in this country. Similarly it was pointed out by members of the legal profession and organizations that assist women who have been stalked.
These organizations that assist women who have been stalked and women experiencing other forms of violence have had their funding cut by the government by 10 per cent this year. Next year it will be 15 per cent. The year following it will be 20 per cent. In other words, the signal is that the government is not supporting these organizations in their very important and critical work.
Not only do we need additional services and at least a commitment to maintain the existing services but we now need to change the law to give the justice system an opportunity to stop this type of behaviour. The Department of Justice in my recollection had one short meeting with organizations such as Elizabeth Fry to get input into this legislation. I remember reading afterward that a number of people attending the meeting felt it was totally inadequate. Maybe they were happy that it was occurring, but one of the reasons we have a rather inadequate piece of legislation before us is that the

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
department did not receive sufficient input from the groups that assist the victims of stalking.
I want to quote from a letter written by the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby, who on behalf of the New Democratic Party brought in a private member's bill that would have been a major effort to combat stalking. She had said that the government bill was drafted without adequate consultation with victims of stalkers and organizations that have helped them and advocated on their behalf. She went on to say that the government bill proposed stalking be considered either an indictable offence with a maximum prison term of five years or a summary conviction offence which is lesser.
My colleague's bill proposed that criminal harassment should only be considered an indictable offence with a five-year maximum imprisonment for the first offence and ten years for each subsequent offence. That oddball from Saskatchewan who stalked Anne Murray would be in prison a good part of or perhaps all his remaining life. She also proposed a maximum of ten years and a minimum of six months imprisonment for people who stalk and harass their victims while subject to a restraining order or a peace bond.
I am quite happy to say that in my province of British Columbia 14 municipalities have passed motions in support of my colleague's private member's bill in favour of strong anti-stalking laws to protect women. That points out the general community interest in the whole issue.
We want to give this matter the priority it deserves. I notice with interest this is an initiative by the government at this late date that attempts to deal with crime against women and children. Yet the government is giving priority to the Mexico-U.S.-Canada trade deal. It seems to be misplaced priorities. We have something that an overwhelming percentage of Canadians oppose, that is NAFTA, and we have something that probably 99 per cent of Canadians would enthusiastically endorse, and the government seems to be taking a rather cavalier and casual attitude toward it all. I suggest to the minister
that the government's priorities are misplaced. The government should put a lot more emphasis on the legislation.
As I said on behalf of my colleagues, we are prepared to stay here all night or over the weekend if it would help move this legislation through to completion before the end of this session of Parliament.
I want to end by simply saying that stalking of women in our society is a very serious problem today. Hundreds and thousands of women are being harassed day after day after day. Their lives are being made intolerable. Stalking, just to remind us all, includes such things as persistently following someone, spending periods of time watching someone's home or place of work, making harassing phone calls to someone, making contact with someone's neighbours or co-workers, contacting and possibly threatening someone's companion or spouse. It goes on and on. It is the kind of thing all of us in the House would surely want to give our full attention to in order to ensure this legislation passes quickly.
In the spirit of moving this legislation along, I have lots more to say but I will say that in committee, at report stage and at third reading. I simply say again on behalf of my caucus that we will do whatever we can to expedite this legislation through the House of Commons and hope that our friends in the other place, the Senate, will give it the same priority.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment and a short question.
I appreciate the very thorough speech of my friend from Kamloops. My friend is not a lawyer but he knows what a false pretence is anyway. It is in the Criminal Code. We could almost call the government a bit guilty of false pretences.
The NDP House leader will know the government has before the House in the dying part of the session a bill on sentencing, a bill on the proceeds of crime and a bill on pornography and children. I saw an article about the Solicitor General and another bill in the paper today on dangerous offenders and keeping them in jail longer. Then it has a bill on psychoactive drugs and this bill. I
May 6, 1993

wonder if the hon. member can tell us what the government is actually going to debate in the next three weeks.
Ele goes to the House leaders' meetings, he looks after that. One would think if the government was really serious it would allocate time so that we could deal with all these matters. The hon. member said in his speech that this government really wants to deal with NAFTA, the North American free trade agreement, and not with crime. I find it to be almost a false pretence for it to say to the Canadian people that it has a program. I can just see it on the campaign trail. The government will say: see all these bills we have, but we just could not get them through the House of Commons.
Who controls the agenda of the House of Commons? Who brings the bills down? What is the government's agenda for the next four weeks when the House will be sitting?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this very serious question from my hon. colleague, because it is a question that a lot of people who are serious about this issue must be asking. After all, this government has been in office now for nearly nine years and here we are, in literally the last four or five weeks of its mandate, it has pushed its mandate right to the nth degree, and it is only now introducing this kind of legislation that people have been calling for to protect women and children and society generally for years and years.
Therefore I question the sincerity of this initiative. On the other hand, let us at least say it is now before us. The litmus test of it all will be to what extent are we going to spend days in the House of Commons, at second reading and third reading, to facilitate this? If the government keeps putting forward pieces of legislation like the North American free trade agreement then that is obviously its priority. In other words, a trade agreement that most people oppose is the priority rather than protecting children from sex offenders, from protecting people's property, from protecting women from stalkers, and on and on as my colleague has indicated.
I want to make this very clear. This place succeeds or fails depending on the willingness to co-operate and what the government considers to be priority legislation.
Government Orders
It introduces the legislation. We can only facilitate its passage or not facilitate its passage.
I want to say that on these bills, which will bring security to Canadians and their families and peace of mind to Canadians generally, particularly women, children and elderly citizens, the New Democrats in the House of Commons will do whatever we have to do to facilitate their passage.
However, the government introduces the legislation. It indicates which bills we discuss in this House and in what order. Therefore I appeal to my friend the government House leader to make these bills a priority, make the children of this country a priority, make the women in this country a priority, make the seniors in this country a priority, and make the victims of crime a priority in this country. If the government does it will have full and complete co-operation from New Democrats in the House of Commons to ensure the passage of this legislation before we rise.

Before recognizing the hon. member, it is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised this evening at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception-National Defence; the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Immigration; the hon. member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley-Softwood Lumber;	the	hon.	member	for
Nanaimo-Cowichan-Fisheries; the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre-Port of Churchill.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-126 is a small step in the right direction and my party will support it.
Mr. Speaker, I might start by pointing out, since you and I are both from Edmonton, that I have something to mention that has been bothering me a great deal. A young woman, married with a child now, came to see me about this issue of harassment about two and a half years ago. You may recall the case. She has been pursued since the age of 11. At the age of 14 her stalker put her in his trunk.

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
She and her family have been living in absolute turmoil. She is now in her twenties. The thing ended when her stalker-I could give his name but it will not be necessary, it has been in the papers in Edmonton-came to her stepfather's house looking for her and basically gouged the eyes out of her stepfather.
Fortunately she was not hurt and her brothers were not hurt. Earlier, on another occasion he came to their home with an axe. He had to be subdued before he was taken away. Basically nothing happened to him in court. He has now been sentenced to nine years in penitentiary. However she is going to have to worry for the next five to six years that he is going to get out again and he may continue to make her life miserable.
There is not a member in this House who does not want to see something done about this issue. Anything that will give people peace of mind is something that members of goodwill on all sides of the House will support.
The problem is that this is simply a band-aid, hopefully a useful band-aid, that we are putting on a very serious problem in society. We can pick up books, we can see videos, we can go to movies, we can buy this serial killer board game that is out now. It is based on some serial killer in the United States. The game comes complete with body bags. The object of the game is to see how many children one can kill. This game is legal. It is considered to be adult entertainment. How many stalkers have gotten the ideas for what they do from what they see on television and what they see in videos or read in books.
All of these things are done in the name of artistic or literary licence. In an age when values seem to be the real problem in many areas, I wonder how many of these 400 women my colleague from Mississauga referred to earlier who have been killed since 1987 were killed because some mentally weak person saw something on television and then went out to try to imitate art? How many catastrophes have occurred to people because of what people have seen on television or in movies?
Bill C-126 obviously has some good features in it. I would like to speak about a few of those. The bill would
prohibit anyone-it says any person but to my knowledge there has never been a man who has been killed by a stalking woman, at least not in my experience as a Crown and defence attorney. To be politically correct and to get by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, we have to say:
any person with intent to harass is now to be barred criminally from
repeatedly communicating with or following another person or
anyone known to that person.
The second thing it does is increase the maximum penalty for the offence to five years in prison. Contrary to what was said by my colleague from the New Democratic Party, a lot of Canadians would like to know why it is not 10 years for somebody who does the kind of things that were done to the young Edmonton woman.
The problem with the existing provisions of the Criminal Code appears to be that the burden of proof is very high. The victims of stalkers have traditionally had a very difficult time convincing the police, clerks at the court so they could swear in information, and judges themselves.
There is a good provision in the bill that deals with bail conditions. If passed, and I certainly hope it will be, a judge can impose a condition that an accused cannot go near a particular place, for example a family home such as the home of this young woman in Edmonton.
That would certainly improve upon section 5(15) of the Criminal Code in which a judge can only require the accused to stay in a particular place but not stay away from a particular place.
As for situations of family violence which are again all too common today, the judge must consider imposing the bail conditions that the accused not go near a particular place and that he not communicate with any person including the victim.
There is a section on conspiracy which I think we will all want to look at in committee because it allows for a husband and wife to be found guilty of conspiring with each other, particularly with respect to children one assumes.
With regard to parental child abduction, right now children are not protected from abduction where there is a valid test of the order, but the abducting parent honestly believes the order to be invalid. This bill would change that and would also cover women who are being
May 6, 1993

battered and who take children with them when they flee.
Now if the children are not being battered along with their mother, the mother could be charged with abduction in taking them with her. An amendment to the code would allow for a defence in such circumstance.
On the section on child abuse the code already says, as you know, that anyone convicted of a sex offence or who is found loitering in or near a school, park, playground or swimming area commits a summary conviction offence of vagrancy. Unfortunately in my experience summary conviction offences rarely carry much more than a fine. In my experience paedophiles are certainly prepared to risk a fine all too often.
One court in British Columbia has found that the present wording of the code with respect to what I just mentioned is unfair. It is a lifetime ban and they feel that is unfair. I certainly hope the Supreme Court of Canada will reverse the B.C. Court of Appeal when the appeal is heard by it. Some people feel the term loitering is too vague also but I would submit that it is not too vague.
This bill before us would allow for up to a lifetime ban on a convicted sex offender from frequenting day care centres, school grounds, playgrounds, community centres, public parks, bathing areas where children are likely to be found, from seeking and obtaining employment that involves a position of trust or authority over children.
The court would have the discretion to tailor the prohibition to each individual or not to impose a prohibition at all. I think that strikes me, at least, as being eminently sensible.
With regard to child witnesses, currently judges tell juries that there is a danger in convicting on the uncorroborated evidence of a child. Bill C-126 would repeal that rule and a child's testimony would have the same weight as an adult's. I think many people who have spent a long time in the courts would feel that probably a child's evidence should often have more weight than many adults'.
Where an accused represents himself in cases of child sexual assault, the judge would now be allowed to appoint counsel for the accused and conduct a cross-ex-
Govemment Orders
amination of the child witness. This bill would allow a judge to permit a friend or relative of the child's choice to be close to the child while testifying. That is designed of course to reduce the psychological trauma which those children often suffer. The person rendering the support could be instructed not to communicate with the child while he or she was testifying.
At present a judge can exclude any or all spectators from a court room if it is in the interest of "public morals or the proper administration of justice." This bill suggests a test be included in the code to strike a better balance between the rights of the public to be present and the interest of the child.
What are some considerations that might be brought to bear when this bill, hopefully very shortly, goes to committee? First the requirement that a victim must reasonably fear for his or her safety could be very problematic. Such a test is traditionally known as the reasonable man test but as I am sure you will appreciate, Mr. Speaker, what is reasonable to a man, especially a large man such as yourself, may be completely unreasonable to a 90-pound woman who is being stalked.
Police in judicial training will be very important if this problem is to be overcome. I might also suggest perhaps a subjective standard would be better than the objective standard that is applied now under the reasonable person test.
Second, a recent study funded by the Ontario Women's Directorate found that of the 551 women murdered in that province between 1974 and 1990, 78 per cent of them were killed by former spouses or companions who had stalked them prior to their deaths. Women's fears are thus well grounded and challenges to convince police, clerks, Crown attorneys and the judiciary of the fear that we are talking about in this bill.
Third, on a matter that has been raised by at least one other speaker since I came in, the question about the motivation of any government that waits until its fifth year. Why would any government wait until there are presumably five weeks more of sittings before we go to an election to introduce this bill? One assumes that the government wants to try to take credit for introducing this bill, but one would wonder why it has not done something about this important issue, which has been an important issue, in the preceding nine years. Similarly, in

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
passing one might ask why it has not done anything about issues such as child pornography during nine years.
There are a host of criminal justice issues, but why has nothing been done about the question of allowing a blood test where a woman has been assaulted? I regret to say that this has happened to one of my constituents. She was raped in her apartment. She naturally wondered if she had been given some horrible disease and possibly AIDS from this assailant and she was told that she had no right to see her assailant's blood test results. There is a similar case in Cowansville, Quebec.
One wonders why on this and on so many other issues we have waited in this Parliament so long before dealing with these issues.
The attitudinal issues are far more important than what we are attempting to do in this bill. How are we going to change the thinking of one-sixth of men? How are we going to change the mind-set of men which has allowed so much family violence to continue to occur, including stalking? Women cannot do it alone and unfortunately, speaking as a former Crown attorney, we cannot do very much by passing a bill like this. At least we can show how strongly Parliament feels about the matter.
The argument that the bill may be used against legitimate strikers and protesters is surely a non-starter. There is already section 423 in the code which outlines intimidation and threatening behaviour. Strikers who engage in such behaviour are already breaking the law.
There have been fears expressed that this bill could be used against women who repeatedly call their ex-husbands for overdue child support payments. That is a valid concern. The government argues that a man receiving such phone calls could not reasonably fear for his safety. The danger is that the police might use the same argument against a woman who is receiving unsolicited gifts, love letters and so on.
Other than extensive police and judicial training it will be difficult to address this issue legislatively and to provide a remedy for the problem we are dealing with.
Some serious consideration should be given to the suggestions of a Quebec coroner, Anne-Marie David,
who investigated two recent stalking-related deaths in her province. She suggested the following: "1) Courthouses and police stations should have part-time or full-time information desks reserved for victims of conjugal violence so that they know their rights and can overcome insecurities about pressing criminal charges. 2) Convictions and bail conditions in conjugal violence should be marked with a special code in police computers to ensure swift action against recidivists. 3) Women should be informed when their violent partner is being released from jail or on bail. 4) Suspects ordered to turn over weapons should be accompanied from court by a police officer who seizes the weapon immediately. 5) Measures should be taken to see men removed from the family home in cases of conjugal violence. 6) Consideration should be given to following London, Ontario's lead in having a social worker accompany police to scenes of domestic violence."
I have a colleague who wants to speak on this bill as well so I will close quickly. The state in the United States with the toughest anti-stalking law is Illinois. I will only quote from part of it, and it is something we might consider perhaps grafting on to the bill that we are dealing with now. Its section on stalking reads:
A person commits stalking when he or she transmits to another person a threat with the intent to place that person in a reasonable apprehension of death, bodily harm, sexual assault, confinement or restraint, and in furtherance of the threat knowingly does any one or more of the following acts on at least 2 separate occasions: (1) follows the person, other than within the residence of the defendant; (2) places the person under surveillance by remaining present outside his or her school, place of employment, vehicle, other place occupied by the person, or residence other than the residence of the defendant.
The second one I would mention is aggravated stalking and I quote again from the Illinois code:
A person commits aggravated stalking when he or she, in conjunction with committing the offence of stalking, also does one of the following: (1) causes bodily harm to the victim; (2) confines or restrains the victim; (3) violates a temporary restraining order, an order of protection, or an injunction prohibiting the behaviour described in subsection -
I hope that when the matter goes to committee, as I gather it will this afternoon, that some of these provisions of the Illinois code will be considered along with the proposed bill on stalking.
May 6, 1993

Mr. Speaker,
I am delighted to be given the opportunity to address this piece of legislation.
The first comment I want to make is that it is about time. It is about time, is it not? Why has this not occurred before? Why wait until now? Clearly and unfortunately it is for election purposes, but still there is some use within this piece of legislation and I am prepared to acknowledge that.
In every single part of the country we all know of incidents where there have been victims of stalking. In Manitoba during the last couple of months, unfortunately, there have been fatalities. One wonders if something like this had come into being some time ago whether or not these fatalities could have been prevented.
Mr. Speaker, I know that you agree with me, we need to take every single measure to protect not only women, but women in particular obviously, but all others in our society who are potential victims of violence. There is nothing that we should not do to prevent that. What is important is not only this piece of legislation which I think is symptomatic of a much larger problem, we need to take an over-all look at violence in society. Time and time again in this House I and other colleagues have spoken about inappropriate use of language on radio and television and acts of violence. We have talked about killer board games. It is rampant and somehow we have failed to meet that challenge.
Not only do we have to take an over-all look at violence in society, I think we have to address the whole question of attitudes. How do we feel about each other? How do we feel about acts of violence as portrayed by the written media, radio or television? What are the changes that we need to make in order to deglorify, to take away that aura that is given to violence and is very often a very positive one?

One of the reasons why I wanted to address this, Mr. Speaker, and I believe that you are probably aware of this is that barely ten days ago, my party, the Liberal Party of Canada, under the direction of its leader, announced a number of measures. I have a booklet here on crime and justice in which the Liberals announce a
Government Orders
series of measures, among them severe measures to combat violence against women and children.
In this announcement, we find some examples, such as making stalking illegal. The Liberal member for Moncton presented a bill on this which could be a model for such legislation. It is a concrete example of how we could proceed. Without wanting to be mean, independent authorities told me that my colleague from Moncton's proposal is better than the government's because it is more specific, it goes farther and is more severe.
Besides this first proposal for severe measures to combat violence against women and children, we also have an amendment to the Young Offenders Act. We toughened up the firearms regulations, which is extremely important because too often, unfortunately, people have been killed as a result of the freedom to own guns in this country. We also want law reform, crime prevention and public awareness. I could give several other examples.
As I was indicating, it is very important to look not only at this legislation, which is important-it should have happened a long time ago-but as well we need to look at the whole phenomenon of violence in an over-all context. We need to change the attitudes of Canadians with respect to violence in the school yard, in the streets, as portrayed by the media, whether it be written, on radio or television.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, because you have been in the chair often when I and other colleagues have spoken about the totally inappropriate use of violence on radio and television. We seem to have become desensitized to violence. Society becomes increasingly violent and we just adapt to it. That is not good enough. That is totally inappropriate. We need to change that.
I am particularly pleased that my party has chosen to announce a series of measures and I just want to refer to some of them. On April 22, less than a couple of weeks ago, the Liberal Party under the direction of our leader announced a crime and justice package. I want to share some of the points that we made in that announcement. I think they are very important.
May 6, 1993

Government Orders
We talked about crime prevention and urban safety, the situation that we now find ourselves in. We talked about ways that we could address that. We talked about young offenders and the fact that we needed to deal with them very differently than we do today. We talked about gun control, recognizing that we need to control the use of guns in a very significant and different kind of way. We talked about prostitution. We talked about the rehabilitation of sex offenders. We talked about violence against women and children. We talked about the proceeds of crime and what to do in those particular situations. We talked about sentencing and rehabilitation, about pornography, about parole, about the court challenges program. That is the one that the government decided to take out. Do you recall that, Mr. Speaker? We would be quite prepared to restore that particular program. We talked about the Law Reform Commission of Canada, another program that we would like to restore. We talked about hate crimes.
I would recommend to you, Mr. Speaker, because I know you are an avid reader, but to your colleagues as well, a profound examination of this whole package. In this package we have a comprehensive approach to the control of crime and to the approach to justice in a much more sensitive and realistic way. I am absolutely delighted that we have taken this initiative.
Yesterday I was speaking about the North American free trade agreement. I said it was probably one of the most important questions in front of Canadians today and that they wanted to discuss it, to hear the various questions addressed and they wanted answers to their questions before government could proceed. Here is an equally important question for Canadians. How will the federal government deal with crime and justice? I believe that there are a number of answers in this package.
Let me make a couple of other brief points with respect to this legislation. I will try not to repeat eveiything that my colleagues have said. Obviously the bill discusses criminal harassment. It discusses as well bail conditions, conspiracy and parental child abduction as well as child abuse. It refers to child witnesses and how they would be dealt with.
I want to make the point that there are some very positive things in the legislation. It is unfortunate it has taken so long for the government to bring it forward. We have indicated that we support this initiative, but at the same time we believe that it could be improved in a number of significant ways. If my colleagues would like
to raise questions I would be absolutely delighted to give them examples.

In closing, I just want to say that in principle I fully agree with this government initiative. I gave some examples that it could use to improve it. I am ready to give some more because, as I said earlier, we have just made a comprehensive announcement about how we in the Liberal Party would deal with this issue that is particularly important for Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (for the Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-85, an act respecting the control of psychoactive substances and their precursors and to amend the Criminal Code, the Food and Drugs Act and the Proceeds of Crime (money laundering) Act and repeal the Narcotic Control Act in consequence thereof, be read the second time and
May 6, 1993

referred to a legislative committee in the Human Resources envelope.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak to this bill today.
This bill, the psychoactive substance control bill, addresses one of the most compelling issues with which society is faced today, the issue of drug abuse.
Members will recall that six years ago the government launched Canada's first ever drug strategy. This was an infusion of $210 million from 1987 to 1992, in partnership with the provinces, designed to take direct aim at a range of areas of greatest need, chief among them the areas of education and prevention, treatment and rehabilitation, and enforcement and control.
This was followed by a second phase from 1992 to 1997 of $270 million, $60 million more, of which the major focus will be on prevention, education, treatment and rehabilitation, in other words, to take people off drugs and to prevent others from starting.
We must keep in mind that every $1 spent on prevention is equal to about $7 for treatment. There will also be an increased emphasis in this second phase on reaching those most at risk, such as young children to high school ages, 11 to 18, or in grades 7 to 13, street kids as well as drop-outs and aboriginals off reserves.
The problem of drug abuse is widespread. According to a United Nations survey, trade in illegal drugs is second only to world trade in arms. To illustrate the point the volume of business in illegal drug sales is more than $5 million per hour, 24 hours a day. Such is the clout of the global industry we are up against in our efforts to control drug abuse in Canada.
Recent statistics reveal that within a single year almost 15 per cent of young Canadians aged 15 to 19 have admitted using cannabis. Moreover the incidence of drug abuse rises considerably among teenagers and young adults who are school drop-outs, unemployed or homeless.
Further evidence shows that over a one-year period 2 per cent of Canadians claim to have used cocaine. That is
Government Orders
500,000 people, enough to fill the Toronto SkyDome 10 times over.
These are formidable figures but what do they mean? What is their significance in sum? They mean heartache and suffering. They mean crippling misery being exacted on those caught in the seamless web called addiction. They mean a rise in crimes such as prostitution, illegal possession, use of firearms, break and enter offences and destruction of communities with threats to the peace and security of our cities, schools and neighbourhoods.
The real importance of these figures goes well beyond the statistical relevance. They translate into millions spent on health care, family welfare, unemployment benefits and disability pensions. Bill C-85, along with the proceeds of crime legislation passed by the House back in 1989, is fully consistent with the strategies and objectives relating to enforcement and control.
Last month, in April, the Minister of Justice introduced Bill C-123 respecting the Seized Property Management Act. That bill would establish a federal program to share the forfeited proceeds of crime with other jurisdictions or, in simpler words, hopefully have the proceeds used by the police forces directly involved in attacking the illegal drug trade. That bill would directly aim at those who seek to profit from exploiting the young and the vulnerable. Together with Bill C-123, Bill C-85 is intended to consolidate and enhance the government's drug policy underlying two current acts of Parliament and to fulfil Canada's obligations under two international conventions relating to the illegal drug trade.
In 1961 the government of the day enacted the Narcotic Control Act. In 1961 and 1969 Parliament passed parts III and IV respectively of the Food and Drugs Act. In essence much of our existing legislative framework is now more than 30 years old. Furthermore, as a signatory to two international agreements on the illegal drug trade, Canada is obligated to the terms of the single convention on narcotic drugs of 1961 and the convention on psychotropic substances of 1971.

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
Consequently the psychoactive substance control bill, Bill C-85, is designed to achieve three prime objectives. The first is to provide the government with the flexibility to better control the import, production, export, distribution and use of psychoactive substances. The second is to provide the mechanisms needed to implement our obligations under international agreements. This relates to the restricted production or trade of internationally regulated substances designed for medical, scientific and/or industrial purposes. The third is to enhance the ability of the police and the courts to enforce the law. The bill currently provides for the seizure and forfeiture of property used in offences involving psychoactive substances.
As a result of royal assent at 4.45 p.m. I believe we will be asked to suspend the debate for a few minutes. I hope the bill at second reading today truly gets the opportunity to go to committee. I am just going to briefly summarize a few points and conclude my remarks to the House.
The bill will try to empower the police through new measures to use warrantless searches where necessary. When the conditions for a search are there and they would have obtained it for the protection of the public, of the people involved or of important evidence, the bill would permit police to do so. The bill would also help us in making new definitions with regard to drugs to better conform to the needs of today compared to 1961 as we are dealing with bills that are 30 years old.
The bill does many of these things. If we take it in conjunction with the other bill I mentioned, Bill C-123, the proceeds of crime bill, the two together would enable us to come to terms with the modern reality of the illegal use of drugs, the way in which these people are destroying the neighbourhoods in our cities, the way in which these people are destroying our young people, and the way in which these people are dragging young women into prostitution in order to live off these drugs.
I commend the bill to the House. It is a good bill. It is worthy of study. There may be some points of division on it. We will want to look at them in committee where I think they can be met. I have much more to say on the bill but I know my time is almost over. I want to make
sure the bill moves forward to committee. I commend it to the House as a bill worthy of support to move it to committee and a speedy passage through to third reading so that before the end of June it can be sent to the Senate and we can start to attack the illegal drug trade and those who profit from it.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-85 is an act that reorganizes the framework to be used in the battle against the production, trafficking and possession of controlled substances.
The charter of rights has rendered obsolete certain laws which were useful in drug enforcement. This bill gives police forces additional powers to undermine producers and traffickers of narcotics. In fact there are many provisions contained in the bill which will significantly impact on the exercise of the duties of police officers as well as the courts.
It strikes me as strange that a bill of such consequence, first introduced last June, has sat around the House for nearly a year before the government decided to move it forward. With barely a month left in this Parliament, the bill seems sure to die on the Order Paper.
The government's motive for letting the bill die is quite transparent. Why would the government want to be drawn into conflict with defence lawyers, some doctors and other health professionals immediately in advance of an election, even if it might be in the best interest of Canadians? It was so much easier to drag it out 'til a few weeks before the close of the House and let it die, all the while claiming commitment to dealing with the drug problem.
For years I have been listening to police officers who have expressed their immense frustration in dealing with drug traffickers. Police feel they could be far more effective if proceeds of crime legislation were improved, a matter I raised with the Minister of National Defence when she was Minister of Justice last year.
At that time Canada had been found guilty of having the highest rate of drug crimes per capita in the developed world. The current framework for the confiscation of property obtained through crime works in favour of the criminal because local police forces face financial
May 6, 1993

obstacles whenever they attempt to seize non-cash assets.
Bill C-85 allows police officers to conduct a search without a warrant in exceptional circumstances where the conditions for obtaining a warrant existed but it would be impractical to obtain one. This would clarify a situation clouded by the fact that warrantless seizures as sanctioned by current legislation have been declared inoperable and in violation of the charter. The provision for warrantless searches in Bill C-85 is said to be charter-proof. Thus a substantial improvement in enforcement procedures has been allowed to collect dust for a year before the government saw fit to bring it to the floor of the House.
Furthermore, Bill C-85 provides for property other than the psychoactive substance or real estate that was used for illegally distributing psychoactive substances for profit to be regarded as offence related property.
This new concept would allow not only for the seizure of drug apparatus and money but for the seizure of other objects. This may include allowing vehicles used in an illegal drug transaction to be seized. By sitting on this legislation the government has squashed this additional weapon that the police could have used in their fight against crime. Bill C-85's new production clause would allow for a wider variety of forms of production to be deemed criminal. This is particularly important in the case of magic mushrooms. Possession is an offence but cultivation is not. Cultivators of magic mushrooms would no longer be able to escape the law were it not for the delay in bringing forward this bill.
Another important feature pertains to chemically altered drugs which may not be listed on the schedule but are psychoactive drugs nonetheless. Bill C-85 would have closed the hole that allows traffickers in these substances to escape justice. Sentencing provisions have also been altered, but since maximum sentences for drug offences are rarely handed out these changes do not merit much attention.
It is a shame that Canada's citizens will be deprived of these improvements by the negligence of this government. In the month that remains the one thing that remains certain is that we will not have time to study this
Government Orders
bill to be sure it is technically sound. We can only doubt that it will even see the light of day.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill as well.
I think there is a lot of hypocrisy going on around here. The drugs that are really big killers are alcohol and tobacco.
It is 50,000 a year.

It is some 50,000 people a year.
This is a throwback bill that goes back to Nancy Reagan's war on drugs. The Prime Minister stood up in this House four years ago and said that he was going there too.
He broke another promise by never doing anything. Now at the end of a dying Parliament, as the hon. member who last spoke so clearly said it, here we are now dealing with a very complicated bill.
I know a little bit about this. I wrote an article about this. It is one of the few articles I ever wrote as a bit of an academic in 1969. It was published in 1970 in the American Journal of International Law. It was on psychotropic drugs and on the original UN Convention.
I tried to look at this in what I would call unhypocritical terms. I introduced in this House a motion and discussions on an international criminal court which would deal with narco-traffickers in different parts of the world. That is something that is really worth pursuing.
Let us look at this bill and we do have it in front of the House. It comes back as the parliamentary secretary said from 1987 when there was a drug strategy to consolidate the Food and Drugs Act and the Narcotic Control Act.
I find it very strange. For the amusement of some of the members one of course could put this bill in committee and bring it back in the House and make a motion with reference since we are consolidating and changing the Food and Drugs Act and the Narcotic Control Act that would deal with the legalization of cannabis. This would of course force the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of the Environment, both former cannabis users, to vote on the bill. I wonder which way they would vote. I suspect they would be far away from the House.

May 6, 1993
Government Orders
This bill is a significant departure from existing legislation. There has been little attention paid to it in the media. There has not been enough attention paid by people in criminology, pharmacology and the health care community.
It is hard to get some comments from people at the Addiction Research Foundation and so on. They seem to just want to let the bill languish and die. Now it is here and now they are going to have to deal with it and eventually it will have to be dealt with.
We hope to hear from these people in committee. We hope to hear from the criminal bar. This changes some of the offences in drug trafficking. There is a different offence for cannabis trafficking. As a matter of fact there is a lesser offence for some cannabis smuggling in one aspect of the bill. This is a long and complicated bill.
Let me give an example. I will just read from my briefing notes on this. The bill creates an integrated, six-part scheduling scheme. Items listed under the Narcotic Control Act, cannabis, cocaine, opiates, et cetera are now listed under schedule I. Items from schedules G and H of the Food and Drugs Act are now listed under schedules II and III though there has not been a carbon copy transfer. So even that has changed.
New substances have been added. For example there is Catha edulis Forsk, or qat, which is used by the Somali community. Some amphetamines have been moved up from schedule II. This is significant in that possession of only schedule I and II substances are offences. Schedule V lists precursors, so it gets more and more complicated.
In fact there will be phrases like: "intended to be used for introduction into the human body which produces a stimulant, depressant or hallucinogenic effect but does not include a precursor." This gets very complicated. How substances are going to be factored into the schedules is quite unforeseen.
I personally agree-and I see my friend, who is a former prosecutor, in the House-that we do have to have another look at the Food and Drugs Act and the Narcotic Control Act. We have to look at that in some detail. They need to be modernized.
I will just end on this. I would like to see the bill examined thoroughly by committee. I wish we had more
time but the parliamentary secretary says that we should come to terms with the modem reality of drags. Then he starts an attack in terms of the war on drugs. That is fine. I believe that we need a healthy society that is basically drug free and which believes in the health of the individual and that is the way we should develop as a human race. However, there is a lot of hypocrisy here and someone has to call it.
The member for Skeena with a bit of tongue in cheek introduced his private member's bill. We have the parliamentary secretary standing up taking a hard line and we have the two leading candidates for Prime Minister of this country who have said, quite honestly, that they smoked cannabis. We have the President of the United States who smoked but did not inhale. We have the U.S. Vice-President who smoked but inhaled. I would hate to go around and do an informal poll of this House of Commons.
Let us cut the hypocrisy. Let us change these laws and update these laws. Let us try to look and see which laws are really working and which are not when we say to the young people of Canada: "We are going to give you an updated modem law that really works and that does not contain a lot of hypocrisy in it."

Madam Speaker, I just started to look at the bill. As one former prosecutor to another former prosecutor, does he not think that section 22 dealing with forfeiture of proceeds of crime is the really major part of the bill? Does he not think, in terms of things like the balance of probabilities test rather than beyond a reasonable doubt, that is where those of us who would like to see a drug free Canada see most of the merit in this bill?

Madam Speaker, I think part of the problem of the forfeiture of proceeds of crime-it is in another bill as well-is that one has to be careful that one does not have the police rely on it. There are some American examples where the police start relying for their budget on the forfeitures from crime. One gets some very strange attitudes that happen.
I would prefer that the police are budgeted to do then-work with the proper and necessary budget and they do not finance directly their budget, or their budget is not dependent, on the proceeds of crime.
May 6, 1993

Adjournment Debate
We want, as the justice committee recommended, the proceeds from crime, including drug crime, to go for crime prevention. Some of the programs that the parliamentary secretary mentioned include drug prevention programs. I think we need drug prevention programs and real ones instead of hypocritical ones.
We need real ones to show some of the dangers of an addiction to drugs and what that really does. My friend has seen what addiction has done to all sorts of communities and people who come before the courts of Canada every day. It is pretty tragic. We want 1 per cent of the budget to go for crime prevention and we want the money from the proceeds to go to crime prevention. That is where we would like it to go.

Madam Speaker, the purpose of my standing today is to petition the government to take seriously the future of the port of Churchill. I know hon. members across are very aware of the fragile nature of some of the ports and the business they do around the world.
The port of Churchill has a very unusual and unique role to play. First, it can serve the eastern and northern part of the European markets. As the Soviet Union has broken up and takes a different shape there are a great number of opportunities for us to use the shipping between Ukraine for example and other republics to develop an even greater level of business.
Second, when we look at the northern part of Canada Churchill has served as a jumping off point for serving these communities through its airport as well as through its port.
The Churchill community has been under threat. It has lost its economic vigour for several reasons in the past 10 years. We on this side of the House would like to see the government make a public commitment to continuing the role of the port of Churchill and to be very aggressive in its support.
We understand there is competition between Vancouver, Montreal and Halifax, for example, on these different issues. I think there still is a unique role. If for some reason the government feels it cannot continue the port of Churchill then I think it should seek out support from the farming community which very much wants to use the route which it calls the Hudson Bay route to take grain out of the northwestern parts of Manitoba and the northeastern part of Saskatchewan.
There is a very well-known advocacy group which I have listened to many times. It makes a lot of sense. Its members met with us. There are ideas they can fulfill. I think it is incumbent upon the government to understand that. If it cannot operate the rural lines and CN wants out, I think it should let other people come in and use that infrastructure. If it does not want to develop the airport at Churchill, step aside and let other people do it. Do not keep people in this holding action and do not cause a slow deterioration of people whose lives are very dependent upon what Ottawa says.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his concern for the future of surface transportation to the port of Churchill.
The rail line into Churchill serves four main functions: export grain, northern re-supply, plus local freight and VIA passenger service to Churchill and other communities. Export grain is the main traffic on the line and the future of the rail line in the port will most likely be determined by decisions on grain traffic.
Churchill is eligible for subsidies under the Western Grain Transportation Act based on an average subsidy of about $20 per tonne. This government has provided around $70 million in western grain transportation subsidies for grain exports through the port of Churchill since 1984.
Over the last 10 years grain exports through the port of Churchill have ranged from a high of 622,000 tonnes in 1983 to a low of only 50,000 tonnes in 1988. Last year 250,000 tonnes were shipped. To recover its operating costs the port needs about 600,000 tonnes.
I am sure the member can appreciate that decisions on grain exports are made by the Canadian Wheat Board on the basis of market considerations. It would not be prudent for the government to interfere in the marketing decisions of the wheat board as it is in the best position to pursue its mandate and maximize returns to prairie farmers.
It should be noted that the Hudson Bay rail line is built in part on discontinuous permafrost. Due to the frequency and unpredictability of resulting sinkholes, the line is expensive to maintain. For safety reasons CN limits grain traffic to boxcars and does not operate grain hoppers on the line.
The boxcar fleet is depleting. Significant capital expenditures will be required to replace the car fleet and improve the line if it is to continue in grain service over the long term.
The Minister of Transport has advised the House that the government does not intend to close the port of Churchill in the immediate future. However, we have a responsibility to look seriously at the long-term future of the rail line and the port in view of the potential capital requirements.
May 6, 1993

The citizens of Churchill and northern Manitoba must be assured that the government expenditures in the region will be able to stand the test of time.

Madam Speaker, I talked about the manifestations of concern, which is being expressed in many ways. I talked about doctors in uniforms speaking out in the last couple of weeks.
The chief of the defence staff at the time, who is an expert peacekeeper and is now our ambassador to the United States, last November expressed grave concern about our continuing commitment, about more soldiers. The Secretary of State for External Affairs in her testimony in mid-February to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade expressed concern about overloading the system.
There has been concern expressed by experts to the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs on the quality and the kind of equipment, the method of deployment, the method of deciding who to send. The litany goes on. Red flags are being thrown up which tell us and which should tell the government that we are having less than a smooth passage in our peacekeeping operations.
Little wonder. Last year at this time we had less than 2,000 troops in peacekeeping. Now we have 4,700, at a time when the Canadian forces are reducing 4,000 soldiers. We heard from testimony yesterday that it is going to be another 2,000.

May 6, 1993
Adjournment Debate
The red flags are up and the trends are going in the wrong direction. We have to be the only country in the world that would commit our troops to a line of fire in foreign territory without so much as a word of formal debate in Parliament. We now have perhaps one of the most crucial peace operations-I would not want to grace it with the term peacekeeping-taking place in Bosnia. We all know that last night it looked as if the peace agreement, such as it was, was not even going to be approved in whatever form, which was better than nothing.
It is my thesis we have now reached a very critical point in this operation. I find it very upsetting as an individual, and I believe I speak for my colleagues on this side of the House, that there does not appear to be one person on the government side who is running the show.
At a time when we have our troops at risk in Somalia and particularly and in Srebrenica, as expressed by the commander there, and at a time when negotiations are being done by the most powerful country in the world for air strikes, the Prime Minister is off on foreign visits. The Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence are not running the show. Questions are being fielded by the government House leader. It is not good enough.
The Canadian public needs to know: what is the mandate of our Canadian forces in Bosnia? They want to know what the rules of engagement are and they want to know what contingency plan the government has in the event that western air strikes take place. These are all legitimate questions. We should have had our first debate when we dispatched our first peacekeeping troops.
Before I wrap up I want to make the point that we must have a debate, whether it is an emergency debate or a debate on the initiative of the government, to consider all the factors that were brought before the House this evening. I would tell members that this is long-term concern. It is not going to go away tomorrow, the next day or the next day.
As you know, Madam Speaker, the House will be shutting down for the summer soon. We do not have a date on it yet. I would implore the House and the government to have in place some institutionalized standing effort so that Parliament can monitor the
peacekeeping operations throughout the summer and the fall depending on what happens after the House recesses for the summer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons and to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as we have said on several occasions, the Canadian Armed Forces are still able to carry out their specific tasks, but with nearly 4,500 members deployed on various missions throughout the world, the resources of our ground forces are somewhat stretched.
The situation, however, is not more critical than we expected, nor does it defy the limits of our defence policy.
Before making any new commitments, the Department of National Defence evaluates each proposal for peacekeeping operations in terms of personnel and equipment requirements and the expected duration of the operation.
Furthermore, the department makes no commitments before considering the repercussions on other Canadian Armed Forces' activities and operations.
At the present time, Canada is able to meet its current peacekeeping commitments. However, considering the rising number of peacekeeping missions and the decision to cut Canadian forces personnel, from now on Canada will have to be very careful in selecting future tasks to avoid compromising existing peacekeeping missions or other Canadian Armed Forces operations.
Consequently, Canada's response to future requests for participation in peacekeeping missions will largely depend on the amounts Canadians are prepared to spend on defence and peacekeeping activities.
These are important questions, and Canadians will have to consider how much they are prepared to contribute to peacekeeping missions. Last fall, Canada, with 1 per cent of the world's population, contributed 10 per cent of UN peacekeepers posted throughout the world.
I think we should also remember that, although the regular forces are now being cut, a corresponding increase in the number of reservists and their integration

May 6, 1993

in the regular forces will help the Canadian Armed Forces maintain their contribution to current operations.
I realize the hon. member is also concerned about the number of reservists currently assigned to peacekeeping missions. Not long ago, one of his colleagues said in the House that 50 per cent of replacement troops in Yugoslavia would consist of reservists. In fact, once the rotation process is complete, only about one-quarter, and not 50 per cent, of our troops in the Balkans will consist of reservists.
The ratio of regular forces to reserves may vary, depending on local conditions and the reaction time available for training.
Every member of the Canadian Armed Forces assigned to a peacekeeping mission is given the training and level of preparation required before departure. In addition to training, information sessions are provided on the culture and political system of the region to which the individual will be assigned.
The hon. member should find these comments reassuring but, as I said earlier, Canadians will have to consider the extent of our future commitment to UN peacekeeping missions. The government is anxious to have this kind of discussion so that we can clearly establish our future involvement in peacekeeping missions.

Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley
Valley): Madam Speaker, last February 22 I had the chance to ask a question in the House of the Minister of Forestry at that time about an expected decision on softwood lumber.
As timing would have it, today we received a decision from the panel that has been studying the whole question as to whether we in Canada subsidize our softwood lumber exports to the United States. Therefore the discussion tonight is very timely.
The decision, and it relates to the question I have presented, was the review by the panel to determine whether we in fact subsidize our softwood exports to the United States. We have had a mixed decision that on a number of points recognizes many of the arguments all
Adjournment Debate
members have made in this House in terms of the way we manage our forest and in terms of the challenge that has been raised by officials and politicians in the United States and the U.S. lumber lobby. However today's decision is also a disappointing one on two points.
The first one is that it really points to the failure of the free trade agreement on this case because all this panel does is review and determine whether the decision of the commerce department in levying the 6.5 per cent tariff on Canadian softwood lumber was made properly. The ruling today does find that in some cases it did not. In another case it was also determined that our stumpage systems are proper and in place.
There are two points that I would also like to raise which are the disappointing parts of the decision today, and one is a very odious decision.
The first is that this refers the decision again for another 90 days and puts off resolving this dispute. Most people in the forest sector are interested in seeing it happen, if I am not mistaken. It has been two years since our country rightfully cancelled the memorandum of understanding, and the issue has yet to be resolved. We have another 90 days which brings us to another panel decision on injury. That, if it follows the same precedent this committee has set, will give another 90 days. At the very least it may not be until the end of this year when a final decision is made.
The odious part of the ruling today is it determined that the raw log export restrictions, and particularly in British Columbia, confer a subsidy on softwood lumber exports to the United States. Clearly nothing could be less correct. The people in British Columbia today are very upset by this decision. It shows that more work is going to have to be done as the commerce department has ordered to review this detail more. People are very upset about this part of the decision.
We have also learned the U.S. lumber lobby which earlier said that it would challenge any part of any decision might move in the favour of Canada to launch an extraordinary challenge under the free trade agreement.
We have reached the point now where I implore and call upon our government to call upon the Clinton administration to drop the tariff now. It is hurting

May 6, 1993
Adjournment Debate
American home builders and it is hurting Canadian forestry workers.
